articles.x: Despite all a visitor can see today, Giribaile is a site still waiting to be uncovered. In recent years excavations have come in fits and starts, for lack of funding for an area that, incomprehensibly, has still not been declared a Site of Cultural Interest. Included in the “Journey to the Time of the Iberians” programme, which the Jaén Provincial Council launched to showcase the province’s great Iberian heritage, Giribaile remains unfinished business for the society and the politicians of Jaén. In the municipality of Vilches, where the Guadalimar and Guadalén rivers meet, Giribaile is an archaeological site of enormous importance. Its 18 hectares hold an Iberian city, a prehistoric sanctuary, an Early Christian or Visigothic monastery and an Almohad castle built after the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa. Above all, Giribaile stands out for holding the remains of the Iberian city of Orisia, razed by the Romans during the Second Punic War. From its height the visitor can also enjoy beautiful landscapes of mountains and olive groves embracing the waters of the reservoir.

Santo Luisico, Santo Manuel, Santo Custodio… Michael Jacobs came to the Sierra Sur to look into and write about the phenomenon of its folk healers, and ended up living here for the rest of his days. The beauty of these mountains and their character also explain why healers flourished here: a geography that encouraged isolation, and with it beliefs and a faith the Church did not control. It was the people who made their own saints, healers who to this day inspire tremendous devotion not only among the people of the Sierra Sur but in many parts of Andalusia and all of Spain. La Hoya del Salobral, also known as the “Joya de Custodio”, is a small hamlet in the municipality of Noalejo, in the Sierra Sur of Jaén. The rugged terrain of this land explains its beautiful landscapes, and it may also explain the flourishing of healers whose legend has spread far beyond the natural borders of these mountains. The most famous of them all is probably Santo Custodio, born in 1885 in La Hoya, where he lived and always received whoever sought his help. His house, on the main street of this small hamlet, is today a place of pilgrimage that opens every Sunday of the year so that the Santo’s faithful can pray to him.

Although the Miguel Hernández/Josefina Manresa Museum is well worth a visit on its own, the privileged surroundings of Quesada make it even more attractive. We can combine the museum with walks to natural monuments such as the Cueva del Agua, the Roman ruins of the Villa de Bruñel or the Atalaya del Infante Don Enrique, from which we can enjoy spectacular views. Beyond all that, the museum takes us through the life of one of the most important poets in our literature, delving into the figure of a humble man, generous and committed to social justice. Among the many personal belongings on display are the typewriter, an Underwood No. 5, on which Miguel typed many of his poems, and the suitcase with which he left Orihuela for Madrid in 1931, determined to make his way on the Spanish literary scene. In Quesada, and housed within the Zabaleta museum, the Miguel Hernández/Josefina Manresa Museum has held the poet’s legacy since 2015. Visitors can enjoy a selection of the Hernández legacy, made up of more than 5,600 items: letters, press cuttings, manuscripts, photographs and personal belongings. They are laid out in five themed rooms matching different stages of the poet’s life: the shepherd poet, the poet in love, the soldier poet, the martyred poet and the poet as myth. Among the museum’s main aims are both to showcase the work of one of the most important poets in Spanish literature and to highlight values the poet stood for, such as social commitment, solidarity and the struggle for social justice and freedom.

We travel to Alcalá to meet Natalia, granddaughter of Francisco, from whom she has learnt the shoemaker’s craft. At over 90, Francisco still practises a trade he learnt at 14 and that has been his livelihood ever since. In his workshop, Francisco made by hand the shoes that would carry many of his neighbours, making the lasts himself too. Having studied Fine Arts, Natalia tells us how she decided to learn her grandfather’s craft. He still comes down to his old workshop every day, in the back room of the orthopaedic shop his son opened.

This path lets us enjoy all the beauty of the Despeñaperros Natural Park, with the landscapes typical of Sierra Morena, a huge mountain range more than 400 kilometres long. On our way to the ruins of the Batán mill we cross a lovely ravine, walking beside the waters of several streams, one of them named after the mill, under a lush riverside forest of ash and alder. In the Despeñaperros Natural Park, past the hamlet of Miranda del Rey, starts the signposted Molino del Batán path. This lovely walk of barely 9 kilometres one way takes its name from the ruins of old mills, or fulling mills (batanes). Of Arab origin, the Batán mill stands in a lovely ravine through which runs a stream covered by a lush riverside forest. On the way we also come across the ruins of a flour mill, and the path ends at a cistern whose water is kept for putting out fires.

The huge rocky beacon of the Peña de Martos, rising above the sea of olive trees of the Jaén countryside, shelters at its foot one of the most historic towns in the province. The Peña, with its castle, features in countless stories and legends of the town of Martos. In this article we also visit the Town Hall, a building that once held the old prison and council chamber, to see the Roman inscribed stones, dating from the 1st century, set into one of its sides. Rising to 1,003 metres, the Peña emerges from the middle of the Jaén countryside to become the emblem of the town of Martos at its foot. Inhabited since the Neolithic, in Roman times the city of Tucci was an episcopal see. Under Muslim rule it changed its name to “Hisn Tus” or “Martus”. Of the castle of the Peña de Martos, built by the Order of Calatrava on its summit, only ruins remain today, the result of systematic plundering and the inevitable wear of time. Completely ringed by a wall, except on the south-west side, where the inaccessible terrain made it unnecessary, the castle took up the whole summit plateau, fitting perfectly to its difficult terrain.

articles.t: Market Gardens of La Redonda de Miradores
articles.x: Market gardens and the gardener’s trade have been closely tied to the city of Úbeda, especially its southern side. From the spectacular viewpoint of the Church of San Lorenzo we can still see the traditionally farmed terraces that have survived the passage of time and the relentless advance of the olive groves, which have almost wiped out the varied landscape this area once enjoyed. The Huerta Grande, the Huerta de la Higueruela and the Huerta de los Sanjuanes still resist, keeping alive here a trade almost as old as humanity. South of Úbeda, the market gardens step down from the foot of the wall that rings the city towards the Guadalquivir valley. The gardens used a network of pre-Romanesque tunnels, known as “minados”, that carried water for irrigation from the aquifers north of the city. Of a landscape of terraces that stretched as far as Baeza, the neighbouring World Heritage city, barely one hundred and nineteen plots of half a hectare, known as “tablas”, survive today. Among them stands out the Huerta Grande, where the Huertas de San Antonio Foundation has led a project to prepare plots, let on a sharecropping basis, to help keep alive the knowledge and trade of the gardeners and the characteristic landscape of this part of the city.

Probably because the province of Jaén stayed loyal to the Republic almost to the very end, a great many air-raid shelters were built, many of which, such as those on Plaza de Santiago or in Arjonilla, have come down to us. In this article, however, we walk the front-line trenches, mainly in Lopera, but also in other towns such as Martos and Porcuna. The best-preserved remains are the trenches beside the Salado stream, about two kilometres from Lopera on the road to Bujalance. It is precisely here that the re-enactment of the famous battle in which the International Brigades took part is held, organised by Lopera Town Council since 2016. Although it is practically unknown, the province of Jaén holds many remains of the war heritage of the Spanish Civil War. Trenches, anti-tank bunkers, machine-gun nests and air-raid shelters still standing today speak of the tragedy of the war. Much of that heritage, and in many cases the best preserved, is in Lopera, which was taken by the rebel army in a battle in which soldiers of the newly formed XIV International Brigade took part. Since 2016 a historical re-enactment of that battle, one of the most important on the southern front, has been held.

La Calle Llana, like the La Alcantarilla district it belongs to, has its origins in the old Arrabal de las Monjas. The street plan of this quarter was completed during the 16th century, with new streets added that gave it a more orderly layout. In its three hundred metres, Calle Llana gathers a great many heritage buildings and much of the city’s history. Its many palaces, now converted into homes, its two convents and above all its look of stone façades with windows framed by great iron grilles still convey the essence of one of the oldest and most emblematic streets in the old town of Jaén. Near the Cathedral, it has its origins in the old Arrabal de Las Monjas. Calle Francisco Coello, popularly known as Calle Llana, is named after one of its most illustrious residents, Francisco de Paula Coello, soldier and cartographic engineer. Stone façades and iron grilles still take the leading role in its many palaces, now restored as homes, most of which belonged to noble and gentry families. Figures such as the poet Miguel Hernández, Juan de Aranda, Eufrasio López and Francisco Coello, as well as many of the painters, architects and master masons who worked on the cathedral, lived on one of the most historic streets in the city of Jaén.

Everything at El Huerto de la Cora has a reason, a story that goes unnoticed by the visitor. You have to decipher the meaning of each element and each inhabitant of this place to understand the true value of what the walls of this old school hold, which, though no longer filled with the laughter and games of children, still stands for life and the future. Thanks to the members of the Huerto de la Cora Eco-cultural Association, a true laboratory is at work here: recovering and preserving local seeds, and some from other provinces, at risk of extinction, and growing plants from other parts of the world considered especially interesting for the climate of the area. In the town of Jódar, in an old school occupied in the early 1990s, El Huerto de la Cora is a reality built on the solidarity and unpaid work of the members of the association that runs it. Its terraces hold a complex mix of promising plant species and varieties of high agro-ecological value, highly singular and many of them almost unknown or at risk of disappearing, which has drawn experts and scholars from countless parts of the world. Today the garden keeps some 400 different varieties, either growing or in its seed bank. Since 2013 the Huerto de la Cora Eco-cultural Association has had official recognition and the use of the land, by unanimous agreement of all the political groups on Jódar Town Council.

articles.c: Monuments, Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: The story of Las Tres Aguas is the story of most of the small hamlets and farmsteads scattered through the depths of the Sierra de Segura. The immense beauty of the mountains also makes daily life hard, which drove many of the people of the area to leave in the 1950s and 60s for the industrial regions of the peninsula, in search of a more prosperous future. In the second Lugares Míticos de Jaén book, Andrés Ortiz Tafur writes about these hamlets and farmsteads, and in particular about Las Tres Aguas and Estanislao Romero, the hero of a lovely story that casts a ray of light on the dark present of depopulation and oblivion hanging over these places. Deep in the Segura, within the Natural Park, countless small hamlets lie almost or completely abandoned today after the mass exodus of the 1950s and 60s. The valley of the Madera river, one of the most beautiful parts of the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, holds many of them: Prado Maguillo, Los Anchos, Venta Rampias, Huelga Utrera, La Conquista, Arroyo Blanquillo, La Peruela and Los Gandones, among others. Las Tres Aguas is a group of farmsteads in a hard-to-reach spot beside the stream that gives it its name. It was once home to some 30 people and met the same fate as most of the farmsteads in the area, its people leaving in search of a more prosperous future. This article is a tribute to Estanislao Romero, who recently fulfilled his dream of rebuilding “El Reservado”, the farmhouse at Las Tres Aguas where he was born.

articles.t: Palace of the Marquises of Viana
articles.x: In the second Lugares Míticos de Jaén book, José Antonio Beltrán describes this palace as one of the architectural wonders of the classicism of the Upper Guadalquivir. Seat of the lordship of Garcíez, this Renaissance building has shaped the urban, economic and social development of the village. Despite many alterations, the palace keeps its original structure: a rectangular plan on two storeys. The arcaded galleries of its two courtyards, around which the palace is laid out, are particularly beautiful. In the historic centre of Garcíez, this palace built in 1548 is one of the finest examples of Renaissance civil architecture in the province of Jaén. It departs from the traditions of the town palace and the fortress palace and can be classed as a rural palace or villa, its form shaped by the farming needs of its lords. Originally built by the heirs of the old lordship of the county of Garcíez, its last occupants were the Marquises of Viana. Declared a Site of Cultural Interest in 2006, its state of repair leaves much to be desired, which is why it is on the heritage red list.

Near the village of La Guardia lie scattered great blocks of sedimentary rock and limestone. On top of them are the tombs that make up the Cerrillo Salido necropolis. According to research, the tombs were cut after the geological movements that made the rock masses sink and break apart. For that reason they follow no particular orientation, but rather make the most of the space available. In the municipality of La Guardia, barely 500 metres from the village, lies this Visigothic site whose tombs are cut into the rock. According to research, the necropolis would extend all around the village, which makes it one of the most important in the country. The first archaeological excavation was carried out in 1954, examining 22 tombs, of which only 7 were intact. The tombs examined were oval and extremely elongated, and followed no particular orientation. Next to this Visigothic necropolis, barely 30 metres away, lies another from the Muslim period.

On the outskirts of Mancha Real, the Peña del Águila has long been a usual leisure spot both for the people of the town and for visitors from other parts of the province. This natural setting, ideal for hiking or mountain biking, has since June 2016 also been a landmark for lovers of unpowered flight. The new flying centre joins the existing one at Siete Pilillas, in nearby Pegalajar, making the province of Jaén an outstanding place for the sport. Opened in June 2016, this free-flight centre makes the province of Jaén, and this area in particular, a landmark for lovers of unpowered flight. To the spectacular landscapes Mancha Real offers as one of the gateways to the Sierra Mágina Natural Park, it adds unbeatable access. Both the take-off and the landing areas can be reached by car, with a return trip to the top of under 10 minutes. Besides unpowered flight, this emblematic area is ideal for other sports such as hiking, running and mountain biking.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Huelga Utrera is one of the many hamlets, practically deserted today, in the Sierra de Segura. In this haven of peace, where nature is lush and the beauty of the landscape dazzles the visitor, many treasures await. We can go down to the Segura river, which passes the hamlet through a spectacular canyon. From here we can also set off on the route to the Cueva del Agua of Poyotello or, as we suggest here, visit the Cueva del Charco or Cueva del Aljibe, where the cold water of a spring that never sees the light awaits. The Cueva del Charco, or Cueva del Aljibe, lies near the hamlet of Huelga Utrera, in the very heart of the Sierra de Segura. From the entrance to the hamlet starts a path, short but with spectacular scenery, that in barely half an hour leads to the cave-spring. We go into the cave through its long, narrow entrance and notice a spring formed by water filtering through the limestone. This small spring, whose water never runs dry, is recorded and documented among the Springs and Fountains of Andalusia.

articles.t: Puente Tablas Iberian Oppidum Visitor Centre
articles.x: Barely 4 kilometres from the city of Jaén lies the Oppidum, or Iberian city, of Puente Tablas. Known since the 1970s, the opening of the visitor centre has at last given this site of incalculable archaeological value the recognition it deserves. Research in recent years has uncovered a ritual linked to the spring and autumn equinoxes, centred on the Puerta del Sol and a female deity, and identified private rooms (banqueting halls, a chapel) and areas devoted to trades (wine presses, ovens, stores). The visitor centre helps visitors understand the customs and daily life of the Iberians and how the settlement evolved. The visitor centre, which opened on 16 February 2016, opened the site to the public. It has two spaces, the entrance halls and the exhibition area, where we can find information on the daily life of the Iberians and a full chronology of the settlement. Through information panels, infographics and multimedia, visitors get an overall view of the importance of this Iberian city, which dates from the 7th century BCE. Having passed 3,000 visitors in its first year, the site is open to the public from Tuesday to Saturday, from 9 am to 3 pm.

Opened in 1874, the La Tortilla mining and metalworking complex brought in the latest technology of its time and became the only works to cover the whole process of producing lead. A complete transport network was designed around it, one of its high points being the branch of the Linares–Puente Genil railway, of which only the trackbed survives. Although some parts are badly deteriorated, the La Tortilla mine and smelter can be considered one of the finest and best-preserved examples of industrial heritage in the province. At the Cortijo de la Vega, in the municipality of Linares, it is the best-preserved mining and metalworking complex in the area. Its seams were already worked on a small scale in the 16th century, although the present complex was built between 1875 and 1885, after the English businessman Thomas Sopwith bought it. It was considered one of the most complete in Europe, since its facilities covered the whole process of producing lead: extraction, smelting and then the making of pipes, sheet and ammunition. After the Civil War the smelter began to decline, along with lead mining in Linares, and it finally closed in 1969. Since mid-2012 it has been listed in the General Catalogue of Andalusian Historical Heritage as a Site of Cultural Interest.

Rafael Zabaleta Fuentes (1907-1960) is one of the most important Jaén artists of the 20th century. Of a marked Expressionist style, some of his works hang in museums as prestigious as those of Buenos Aires, New York and Tokyo. Most of his legacy, however, is in his home town, Quesada. There, in the museum named after him, a monographic exhibition of his work is on show, with 114 oil paintings, 11 watercolours and 500 drawings. Opened in 1963, the Zabaleta Museum is in the beautiful town of Quesada, the painter’s birthplace. It is a monographic gallery devoted to the renowned Jaén artist, where we can see a varied selection of his artistic legacy. Having opened barely a few years after the painter’s death, the museum was refurbished in 1992. Besides the work of Rafael Zabaleta, the museum’s galleries hold paintings by masters such as Picasso, Miralles, Miró and Tàpies, who paid tribute to Rafael by donating their works.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: To reach the recreation area we start from Segura de la Sierra and head for Navalcaballo along the JV-7032 and JF-7016 roads until we come to a couple of junctions, where we carry on south along the JF-7038 towards the Forest Defence Centre and Río Madera. About 16 kilometres from our starting point we reach the Los Negros recreation area. Superb facilities await us there, sheltered by a spectacular black pine forest where ferns also abound, thanks to the damp brought by the nearby Madera river. Listed as a controlled camping area, this recreation area lies in the valley of the Madera river, in the heart of the Sierra de Segura. The shade of the black pine forest and the nearby river make for a cool, damp atmosphere, especially welcome in the summer months. Its full facilities, with toilets, tables, drinking fountains, barbecues and more, make it a superb choice for the weekend. From here we can set off on many walks, joining stretches of the GR-247 that show all the beauty of the Cazorla, Segura and Las Villas Natural Park.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Poyotello is a small hamlet near Pontones where, besides its singular beauty and spectacular landscapes, the spectacular Cueva del Agua of the Segura river awaits us. In scientific terms this enormous hollow is a karst spring whose walls ooze the water filtered down from the upper parts of the mountain. Going inside, in the deepest part we can see the remains of a “cenajo”, a structure used to keep livestock under the shelter of caves or rock overhangs. From the Cueva del Agua we can carry on along the path, which always runs alongside the Segura until it reaches the hamlet of Huelga Utrera. At the entrance to Poyotello, a small, singular hamlet in the municipality of Santiago-Pontones, starts a path that leads steadily downhill to the Cueva del Agua. As we go down, the murmur of the still young Segura river grows louder as it runs through a spectacular canyon. In about 40 minutes we see the Cueva del Agua on our right, an enormous hollow whose walls ooze water all year round, forming a great pool on the floor. The karst process explains how water filters through the limestone from the highest parts of the mountain and “springs” again from the walls of the cave.

articles.c: Nature, Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: In the hamlet of Los Anchos, the Alma Serrana Ecomuseum has been open since 2002 to gather and showcase the natural and cultural heritage of the Sierra de Segura. Within its walls we can learn the history of the mountains and their people, their customs and their work, everything about a way of life closely tied to nature and to making use of its resources. In the hamlet of Los Anchos, in the very heart of the Sierra de Segura, stands this singular ethnological museum. Thanks to the work of the cultural association La Esparteña and the determination of José Laso Flores, the museum opened on 18 May 2002. The museum is housed in an old 19th-century house, restored to show as faithfully as possible the original layout and decoration of the home. Other sections of the museum recreate a shepherd’s house and a rural school, and have rooms gathering tools used in farming and woodwork.

The Peña del Águila range lies in Mancha Real, at the gateway to the Sierra Mágina Natural Park, a town not far from the provincial capital. Although it does not exceed 1,500 metres, it offers superb views over almost the whole province: from the summit of the Mojón Blanco we can make out nearby Mágina, the Sierra Sur and La Pandera to the south-west, Pegalajar and its Serrezuela to the west, and on clear days even Sierra Nevada. Although it lies outside its boundaries, the Peña del Águila range can be considered the gateway to the Sierra Mágina Natural Park. With its recently improved paths, it offers an easy circular route, though with quite a climb, that rewards us with wonderful views of many parts of the province. On the way up we reach the top of El Morrón (1,355 metres) and the Mojón Blanco (1,495 metres). From the latter, very close by, we can see the Almadén and the Aznaitín, standing for Mágina. A good way to end the walk is to go down to the Peña del Águila recreation area, which has a viewpoint with spectacular views of the nearby town of Mancha Real.

In the old town of a city declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO stands one of its most peculiar monuments: the Water Synagogue. Its peculiarities begin with its very location, since it stood literally next door to the house of the Inquisition. As for its layout, today we can enjoy the six rooms of the original building: the inquisitor’s room, the courtyard, the main hall, the women’s gallery, the ritual bath or “mikveh”, and the cellar and ovens. Of them all, the ritual bath, or mikveh, is the most characteristic. It was used for purification baths, in which the whole body had to be immersed in its water. Discovered by chance in 2007 during work on what was to be a block of flats, the Synagogue has been open to the public since February 2010. Its discovery halted the original project, and its preservation and restoration became the developers’ top priority. In the heart of the old town of Úbeda, according to research its origins go back at least to the 14th century. The Synagogue is made up of six clearly distinct rooms: the inquisitor’s room, the courtyard, the main hall, the women’s gallery, the ritual bath or “mikveh”, and the cellar. Above all stands the “mikveh”, used for ritual purification baths, in whose centre is a hollow cut into the rock where water springs naturally. The mikveh and the seven wells in the Synagogue, all connected to one another, show how important water was to this place.

The Fuenmayor recreation area is one of the most popular spots not only in the Sierra Mágina Natural Park but in the whole province. Right next to it starts a path that, in a steady, moderate climb, leads to the Zurreón waterfall. Along the way we see a mix of landscapes: cherry and almond orchards, planted pine woods and holm oaks, which prevail for much of the way alongside the scrub. Following this path we can climb one of the highest peaks in the province, the Peña de Jaén, and from there follow the ridge to Pico Mágina, the roof of the province at 2,164 metres. Barely a kilometre from the Fuenmayor recreation area, along the path of the same name, we come to a lovely waterfall called the Zurreón. Because of its altitude, it is often completely frozen in the winter months. Following the path we enjoy spectacular views of the cherry and almond orchards that abound here and, as we gain height, we can make out the village of Torres and the mountains around it. Although the area can be visited all year round, spring is the best time, when both the cherry and the almond trees are in blossom, making the landscape even more beautiful.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: To speak of the Campos de Hernán Perea is to speak of one of the most spectacular landscapes there is to enjoy. A place to travel back in time and cut yourself off almost completely from civilisation. At about 1,700 metres up, the harsh winter weather leaves these 5,000 hectares practically uninhabited, in the keeping of the shepherds who still ply their trade in the mountains. Crossing the plateau, always avoiding winter, is a must for any self-respecting hiker and an experience impossible to forget. With this second article we end our journey across the spectacular high plateau of the Campos de Hernán Perea. Along the way we take in the grandeur of emblematic places such as the Poyos de la Mesa, the Salto de la Novia and the Estrecho de los Perales. We meet the Galapán pine, a black pine more than 400 years old and 40 metres tall, without doubt the most emblematic tree of the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park. We end our visit to the plateau at the hamlet of Don Domingo, near Santiago de la Espada.

articles.t: Sanctuary of the Virgen de la Villa
articles.x: On a rocky hill, the Sanctuary of the Virgen de la Villa can be clearly seen from a distance. The present church owes its Neo-Baroque style to the architect Andrés Pajares, who rebuilt it after the serious damage it suffered at the start of the Civil War. Above it all stands the bell tower, built on an old turret of the wall that protected the town of Martos; it is the only part that survives of the remodelling carried out by Francisco del Castillo in the 16th century. Right after the Christian reconquest, the Sanctuary of the Virgen de la Villa was built in Martos. On a rocky hill, the Sanctuary was remodelled in the 16th century by the renowned architect Francisco del Castillo, when the bell tower was also built on a turret of the old wall that protected the town. After serious damage in the Civil War, the Sanctuary was completely rebuilt in the 1940s, leaving the bell tower as its only original part. The church houses the image of the Virgen de la Villa, perpetual mayor of Martos.

articles.t: Old Town of Segura de la Sierra
articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: A must-stop, Segura de la Sierra is without doubt one of the most beautiful villages not only in the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park but in the province of Jaén and all of Andalusia. Its spectacular castle and Arab baths are the crowning touch of an old town of small, steep streets climbing the slope of the hill the village stands on. In this article we take in the singular beauty of its streets and other emblematic places such as its square bullring, the Imperial Fountain of Charles V and the parish church of Nuestra Señora del Collado. With barely 2,000 inhabitants, Segura de la Sierra stands 1,240 metres up in the very centre of the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park. The village reached its height under Arab rule, a time recalled by its spectacular castle and its Arab baths, places we have already shown you here. Today we invite you on a walk through its narrow, steep streets: a lovely route past the house where the poet Jorge Manrique was born, the Imperial Fountain of Charles V, the parish church of Nuestra Señora del Collado and its square bullring. Four of the gates that led into the town through the wall can still be seen today: Catena, Gontar, Orcera and the Puerta Nueva, rebuilt in the 16th century.

articles.c: Nature, Castles and Fortresses, Despeñaperros Natural Park
articles.x: Of Islamic origin, the main purpose of this fortress was to control the Muradal or Losa pass, the only accessible way from the province of Jaén to the Meseta. The Almohads abandoned the castle as the Christian troops advanced, and they occupied it just three days before the famous battle of Las Navas de Tolosa. Declared a Site of Cultural Interest, its present ruined state does not reflect the historical importance of this fortress. In the municipality of Santa Elena, in the very heart of the Despeñaperros Natural Park, this castle controlled the Losa or Muradal pass, the link between Andalusia and La Mancha. Its strategic position made it one of the protagonists of the most important battle of the Reconquest, since the Christian troops occupied it barely 3 days before the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa. Sadly, this fortress of Islamic origin is now in complete ruin, after suffering great damage when a firebreak was cut in the early 1990s.

articles.c: Nature, Sierra de Andujar Natural Park
articles.x: Considered the oldest in Spain, the Romería de la Virgen de la Cabeza takes thousands of pilgrims every year through the beauty of the Sierra de Andújar Natural Park to the Cerro del Cabezo, where the Sanctuary stands. The traditional route from the town of Andújar to the Sanctuary is called the Camino Viejo. The “San Ginés - Lugar Nuevo” path follows much of it, leading to one of its most emblematic spots, the famous Pilgrim’s Viewpoint. The Pilgrim’s Viewpoint lies on the Camino Viejo, the traditional route the pilgrims take from Andújar to the Sanctuary of the Virgen de la Cabeza. To visit it we follow the path that starts at the Hermitage of San Ginés and ends at a small palace, known as Lugar Nuevo, used by several heads of state since the time of Alfonso XIII. This path takes us through some of the most spectacular parts of the Sierra de Andújar Natural Park, with lovely views of the Jándula valley. The Pilgrim’s Viewpoint opens up a full panorama of the Cerro del Cabezo, with the Sanctuary clearly visible on its summit.

The La Serrezuela circular path is an easy loop, ideal for doing with children, and of singular beauty. We can start from different points, the Siete Pilillas viewpoint or the village of Pegalajar, joining a well-kept path along which we enjoy lovely views from its many viewpoints, such as the Peña de los Buitres. The walk also brings us closer to the history of Pegalajar: its rural architecture in the chozos, its role as a natural border between the Christian and Nasrid kingdoms in the remains of the Pedregosa watchtower, and its most remote past in the rock paintings of the Serrezuela shelter. To round off our day in the country, we can have a picnic in the Siete Pilillas recreation area, a place famous for gliding and other unpowered flight. In this second instalment we cover the climb to the Peña de los Buitres and its survey point, then carry on to complete this circular path. From quite a distance we can already make out the spectacular cliffs of the Peña de los Buitres, to whose top we can climb to enjoy the most spectacular views of the whole route from a purpose-built viewpoint. Carrying on along the path towards the survey point, we come across the contadero, a natural narrowing between two rocks that helped shepherds count their flock, since the animals had to pass one at a time. We end our climb at the survey point, 1,126 metres up, where the Pedregosa watchtower once stood, with overwhelming views. From the survey point we carry on to the Siete Pilillas recreation area, where we started, having enjoyed a lovely, easy route, ideal for families.

Paco and Pepe are the sixth generation of their family to work as blacksmiths. They welcome us into their workshop, in the very centre of the Renaissance city of Úbeda, next to the Plaza de San Lorenzo, in a 17th-century building. There they shape the iron into railings, gates and artistic pieces that have won several national competitions. Hard as it is to make a living from a craft, these two men from Úbeda keep their workshop doors open, inviting in everyone who passes so they can discover the process of a job that is hard but, as they tell us, enormously rewarding. We talk with them while they shape a table, the latest order they have received. Then we walk through an exhibition of their work on the upper floor of the building; there, among beautiful handmade pieces, Paco shows us one of his best-kept treasures: one of the five keys of the city of Úbeda, made by his grandfather. We invite you to discover their story, which is the story of the blacksmith’s craft in Úbeda.

The castle of the Peña Negra was conquered more than 70 years after the Christians took Quesada. How hard the fortress was to conquer made the place glorious, and it became a centre of devotion in the area. That led to the building of the Sanctuary, whose exterior keeps much of its original 16th- and 17th-century design. Its interior, however, departs further from the original, after the restoration carried out to repair the damage suffered during the Civil War. Today it is one of the most venerated places in the whole province, and every September thousands of devotees come to venerate the image of the Virgen de Tíscar, patron saint of Quesada and of the Adelantamiento of Cazorla. In a spectacular setting, at the foot of the castle of the Peña Negra and above the Cueva del Agua, stands the Sanctuary of Tíscar. Architectural remains place the origin of the church in the 16th century, although most of the building was put up in later centuries. It was badly damaged in the Civil War and owes its present appearance to the restoration of the mid-20th century. Probably the most venerated place in the whole Upper Guadalquivir district, on the first and last Sundays of September it receives pilgrims, who come by night to the Sanctuary and the Cueva del Agua to worship the image of the Virgen de Tíscar.

We begin at Barranco de Valdeazores path from the forest house of the same name. We will get here via the A4 Cadiz bound, at the 245 Kilometre. We will leave the car here to start an espectacular walk to Collado de la Aviacion Shelter, to end up at The Organs Natural Monument viewpoint where we will enjoy a wonderful view of Despenaperros coomb. Arguably one of the most amazing paths in this Natural Park, one of the most espectacular and less known of the Province of Jaen. Barranco de Valdeazores path will take us to this shelter at the heart of Despenaperros Natural Park. At the beginning of our journey we will cross a plantation forest, finding local vegetation such as holm oaks, cork oaks, gall oaks and holly  as we are going higher. We will get to Collado de la aviacion shelter after a crossing. It is well known for being the watching place of Franco’s bombers during the Civil War. Today the shelter is used by shepherds and hikers. Our trip ends in the amazing The Organs Natural Monument viewpoint, a group of enormous rock columns similar to the tubes of a huge organ, hence the name. From this viewpoint we can enjoy the lovely grandscape, witness of the origin of this part of the Earth inhabited by men since prehistoric times.

Viajamos hasta Los Villares –municipio de 6.000 habitantes situado junto a la capital– para conocer a Francisco, quien lleva más de 45 años dedicado al trabajo del mimbre. Nos reciben en un pequeño taller situado en el piso bajo de su propia casa, donde Francisco, su hermano y otro compañero pasan 10 horas todos los días manteniendo vivo un oficio al que ya poca gente se dedica en el pueblo, pese a que como nos explica Francisco en la entrevista “en las décadas de 1970 y 1980 más del 80 por ciento del pueblo se dedicaba a la cestería, aquí no había paro ninguno”. Nuestras dos horas de entrevista transcurren sin que estos artesanos dejen de trabajar mientras hablamos, con sus manos trenzando el mimbre sin error, sin que les sea preciso mantener fijas la mirada ni la atención. “Son ya muchos años” nos dicen.

La Pandera is one of the icons of Sierra Sur and the Province of Jaen. It is 1872 metres high providing spectacular views of almost the entire Province of Jaen, and in clear days, even Sierra Nevada, la Sierra de Alhama and la Serrania de Ronda. It is possible to get to the top by car following the A-6050 road linking Jaen to Valdepenas de Jaen and Castillo de Locubin. However, if we would like to fully enjoy the magnificence of one of the most beautiful natural environments in the whole Province, the best thing to do it’s to walk our way to the top. There are many routes starting from different locations, but we recommend to take the one via Puerto de las Coberteras. La Pandera is 1872 metres high, it’s the ceiling of Jaen’s Sierra Sur. It offers spectacular views of Quiebrajano, Sierra Sur, Jaen city, Magina, Cazorla and even Sierra Nevada. It is located between the limits of Los Villares and Valdepenas de Jaen. There is a road (the gradient of the slope increases more than 15%) that provides with direct access to the top. This is the main reason for it to be included as the main mountain stage in the last editions of vuelta ciclista a Espana. For fans of trekking, the route from Puerto de las Coberteras, via Puerto de la Nava and Pena del Altar till the top of La Pandera, is one of the most beautiful ones in the Sierra Sur and generally in the whole Province. At the top there is a Red Territorial de Mando - telecommunications military base- built in the 50s with support from the USA army. There are barracks, heliport, several buildings and guard posts. It is not in use anymore. Despite the refurbishment in 2011 to be used by tourists, the place is in a regrettable neglected state.

In order to get to Las Majadillas Lookout, starting point of our route, we will follow A-420 from Marmolejo towards Cordoba. Once we have crossed the river Guadalquivir, we will take right on the crossing following JV-5001 for 7 kilometres until we get to the lookout. From this point there are 6.7 kilometres, around 2 hours walk, of a lovely path surrounded by one of the most iconic landscapes of Sierra Morena. La Centena allows us to travel through an area where native species,  such as holm oaks, have been living here since time immemorial. In addition to bumping into native flora, during this walk we will be able to see sheeps, cows, bulls and horses grazing on the vast lands of the mountain range farms. We will start our way from Las Majadillas lookout, where we will find a recreational area and great views from the nearby village of Marmolejo. This path, almost 7 kilometres long, takes us along a curved shaped landscape scattered with the native holm oak forest typical from Sierra Morena. The forestland that we will see in our way, is completed by eucalyptus, cypress, stones pines and resin pines, and the typical Mediterranean low shrub vegetation. We will enjoy wonderful views of Yeguas reservoir and we will see livestock as we cross different farms until we get to the shrine of San Jose, only a niche and part of the wall preserved today.

articles.c: Nature, Sierra de Andujar Natural Park
articles.x: Sierra de Andujar Natural Park is specially well known for being the last place where Iberian lynx can still be found. However, beyond this amazing fact that makes it different from any other park, we need to add the stunning mountain ranges, a luxury to the senses. The area we are approaching today, El Encinarejo, is considered as the main entrance to the park, and the path that runs through it is one of the busiest. The river Jandula makes alive a beautiful riverside wood, and walking through it we will see the wide variety of trees and animals that live here. We will finish our walk at the dam of Encinarejo, a little reservoir used in the production of electric energy. El Encinarejo’s recreative area is the starting point of a path which runs through one of the most iconic areas of this Natural Park. We will start this unforgettable walk by crossing Puente de Hierro (Iron Bridge), considered as the main entrance to the Park, and we will always walk next to the river Jandula. Marking the river course there is a beautiful riverside woodland made of ashes, alder trees, oleanders and a willows escorting us in our way. If we are lucky we could see some of the otters that live here together with other species such as herons or grebes. We also need to add some of the main examples of Iberian fauna such as, the lynx, the deer, the imperial eagle, the wolf and the black vulture. There are several wildlife observatories along the path, to watch animals in general and specially birds. Our path ends at the dam of Encinarejo reservoir - that looks like a natural lake. It is also possible to walk around it.

Tiscar Castle or Castle of Penas Negras, is placed in the middle of a beautiful and steep place, next to the Shrine of the Virgin of Tiscar and not far from Cave of the Water. It was practically an impregnable fortress due to the enormous difficulties to get to its location, due to the steepness of the terrain. There are a wide range of legends referring to this, such as the appearance of the Virgin Mary to help the Christian siege. This ‘fact’ triger the building of the Shrine of the Virgin of Tiscar in the surroundings of the castle itself. Tiscar Castle is located in a magnificent and steep rock, in an area known as Penas Negras. The first records of this Berber origin fortress date back to AD 876. There are plenty references, especially during the time of the muslim rule. Its strategic position made Christian and Muslim rule to alternate in several occasions until the year 1319, when it gets under the rule of the prince don Pedro de Castilla. Some of the walls and the donjon can still be seen today. The donjon was built by the Christians in the 14th Century after conquering the castle. However, Pena Negra, a huge rock in the middle of the castle premises, was used as a Donjon before.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Take the road A-6206 from Quesada towards Pozo Alcon and approximately 13 kilometres after, you will find on the left hand side Tiscar’s Shrine. There is a little path from here till the famous Cave of the Water, also known as the Virgin’s Cave. This canyon, shaped by the Tiscar stream, is one of the first natural grottos found in the country. It was declared Natural Monument by Junta de Andalucia because of the stunning beauty, including the water features such as sources and waterfalls. Quesada Town Hall turns the cave into a magnificent stage for ethnic music every August since 1993. This spectacular calcarean cave, well known for its beauty and for being one of the first natural grottos found in the country, it is halfway between Quesada and Pozo Alcon. It was declared Natural Monument by Junta de Andalucia. Tiscar stream created this beautiful canyon shaping the rocks for centuries. We can get to the cave through a 10 metres long tunnel excavated in the rock. Then, we will climb up the stairs to get to the upper part to be able to see the amazing views. Legend has it that in this place the Virgin appeared in 1319 to Mahomad Abdon Tiscar’s King. For this reason it is also known as the Virgin’s Cave.

articles.c: Monuments, Castles and Fortresses, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: There is a deviation towards Tiscar mountain port on the road to Quesada. In that place, over 1180 metres high, we can find the round don Enrique Watchtower. This tower is over 10 metres high allowing us to see a vast portion of territory around it. It was mainly used to check the movements of the troops on the way to the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada, raising the alarm among the closeby castles - Tiscar or Quesada - in dangerous situations by using smoke signals. We can still see today 2 coats of arms in the facade; in one of them - the best preserved one- there are 2 castles and 2 Calatravan crosses, possibly the coat of arms of Prince don Enrique. This spectacular over 10 metres high round tower is located at Tiscar mountain port, just a few kilometres away from Quesada. It was built at the end of the 13th century under the orders of don Enrique - son of Fernando 3rd the Saint and brother of Alfonso 10th the Wiser. It was mainly used to check the troops on their way to the Kingdom of Granada. After the restoration a metal ladder allows us to get inside through the original door, located 3.5 metres high. From this privileged location - over 1183 metres over sea level- we can see the municipality of places such as Baeza, Torreperogil, Ubeda, Santo Tome, Villacarrillo or Iznatoraf.

The recent history of Marmolejo is linked to its water and hot springs. With less than 4000 inhabitants, this small town dedicated mainly to farming, used the term ‘ the 3rd harvest’ to refer to all the economical improvement generated by the spa. Marmolejo’s hot springs were both kept in bottles and also used as a spa for 185 years till the Guadalquivir river floods ended up with the place. It was reopened again in 2004 by the Town Council, but a new flood from the river would end up with the dream just 5 years later. The first written recording about the medicinal water of Marmolejo dates back to 1701, but it won’t be until the 19th century that this little town and its hot spring would be popular. Marmolejo, with less than 4000 inhabitants, became the favourite place for the wealthy Spanish people. The spa triggered the economic revolution in town; 3 cinemas, 4 casinos, 7 hotels, theatre and several shops were opened. It is in 1950 that the spa starts to decline, provoking the closure of several hotels when the number of visitors decreased. In 1997 the flood of the river Guadalquivir destroyed a big part of the spa and mixed with the hot spring ending up with the closure of the spa. In 2001 the Town Hall acquired the spa and reopened it in 2004. However in 2009 new floods by the river Guadalquivir destroyed the spa again, and left it in the state that you can see in our report.

The origins of this fortress go back to the 12th century, when the Almohads fortified the place by building several towers to protect it against the Christian troops. It was conquered in 1244 by Fernando the 3rd, and passed to the Calatrava Order’s hands in the 13th century. It was shaped in its current structure by the “Calatravos” who were in charge of its refurbishment. Later on, in the 17th century, the South wall was demolished in order to join it to the Marquis’ palace. As a curiosity, it is worth mentioning that the well known name of the castle is not due to wars or battles that took place among its walls, but rather to Troubadour Macias legend who was locked and killed at the Homenaje tower because of love. Arjonilla’s Castle is from Almohad origin, It was conquered in 1244 by Fernando the 3rd’s troops. In the 13th century it passed to the Calatrava Order’s hands to refurbish it. Above the whole castle it stands out the Homenaje tower. Square plan tower, 5 meters wide x 17 metres high. It is possible that the castle had another Homenaje tower, lost today. However this castle is not well known for being the scene of wars and battles but rather for the famous Troubadour Macias legend, that inspired Larra or Lope de Vega among others. Legend has it that in the Homenaje tower Troubadour Macias was a prisoner that lived and died there, because he was in love with dona Elvira.

articles.t: Museum of Navas de Tolosa’s Battle
articles.x: Navas de Tolosa’s Battle is considered a changing point in the Christian Reconquest. Lots has been written about it and it is one of the most epic battles ever. Almost double in size, the Almohad’s army was defeated by the Christian Alliance in mid July 1212, which get back Vilches, Ferral, Banos de la Encina and Tolosa among others. Despite the importance of this victory, the Reconquest was not completed till more than 2 centuries later. The Museum of Navas de Tolosa’s Battle, opened in 2009, offers a didactic approach to the historical facts related to the Battle’s time. On the 16th July 1212 took place not far from Santa Elena one of the key battles for the Reconquest. The Christian alliance’s army, having half soldiers than the enemy, defeated the Almohad Caliph Muhammad an-Nasir’s troop. Despite the big difference in size, the victory was decisive, starting the decline of the Muslim empire and beginning the final stage of the Christian Reconquest. In 2009 the Museum of Navas de Tolosa’s Battle opened on the grounds that witnessed the battle, right in the middle of Despenaperros’ Natural Park.

articles.t: Santuario de la Virgen de la Cabeza
articles.c: Nature, Monuments, Sierra de Andujar Natural Park
articles.x: Virgen de la Cabeza’s Shrine during the last week of April is the destination of thousands of pilgrims in one of the oldest pilgrimages in Spain. The last Sunday of April the procession of the Virgen de la Cabeza - known as “Morenita”- is celebrated here since 1505, being this shrine the centre of the event. Cofraidias (religious brotherhoods) from all over the country, decorated with flags and coats of arms all the path from Andujar till the Shrine, where they go to honour the image of the Virgin. The shrine keeps the image of the patron saint of Jaen’s Diocesis and the City of Andujar. It is located at the heart of Sierra de Andujar’s Natural Park, on top of the commonly known as “Cerro del Cabezo”. It was built between 1287 and 1304, but it has suffered multiple refurbishments since then - the most important during the 16th century - and almost a full reconstruction after the civil war. It has been guarded and opened to worship since 1930 by the Trinitarian Order. It is specially decorated to its best during the last weekend of April to celebrate one of the most important pilgrimages in Spain. In 1936 a group of 200 rebel guardias civiles sheltered in the shrine, resisting inside a 9 months siege by the republican army. This event, that was taken to the cinema, ended up with the destruction of the Shrine.

articles.c: Nature, Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: After our first visit to Segura’s Castle - in which we checked the inside and enjoyed the amazing views that it has to offers - we will contemplate its stateliness from the outside on this occasion, searching for nearby places that show us the walls protecting the old Segura village and the several towers emerging on the way to access the 4 gates to the Medieval Segura. Catena, Gontar, Nueva and Orcera are the gates’ names, however only the first three can still be seen today. In this second part we will pay attention to the outside of the castle and the towers surrounding it - via different perspectives from closeby locations. The castle was linked to the village by a fence which was also used for proctection. Several towers were built in this wall. One of them was the Water Tower, which got its name from a hot spring that could be accessed through the upper part of the tower. A big part of the walls surrounding old Segura are still preserved today, together with the 4 gates to access the town: Catena - the best preserved one -, Gontar, Orcera and Nueva gate, which was rebuilt in the 16th century.

This chapel is one of the emblems of Torredonjimeno, because it holds the image of Virgin de la Consolacion, the patron saint of the town. It was built in the 15th century not far from the cave where the image of the Virgin was found, to which Diego Lopez Pacheco prayed before his victory over the Muslim army. It was later on refurbished in the 17th century. Visigoth remains had been found inside leading us to think that it might have been originally founded in the 7th century. Every 8th September the Chapel is a pilgrimage destination. Located less than 2 kilometres away from Torredonjimeno, this chapel holds the image of Virgin de la Consolacion, the patron saint of the town. Around the year 1450 the image of the Virgin was found inside a nearby cave. Diego Lopez de Pacheco prayed to her before his battle with the Muslim army. After winning the battle, Diego Lopez de Pacheco commissioned the building of the present chapel on the site of the previous one. It’s got a cross plan and it is made of just one nave. The sacristy is in gothic style and in the quarry facade two bodies can be distinguished, there is an niche with an image of the Virgin on the top one.

articles.c: Nature, Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Iznatoraf, once a very important Islamic Medina, has preserved the essence of it in the narrow and crooked structure of the streets, making a beautiful historical old town. Its name came from the Arabic Hisn-al-Turab, and it is located on Las Villas Shire, on top of a mountain over 1,000 meters high. The facades and medieval arches are decorated with limitless plant pots creating a very special picture in the old town. It was declared Historical-Artistic Complex in May 2012. It belongs to The Villas Shire, located on top of a mountain over 1,000 meters high. Its name come from the Muslim word Hisn-al-Turab. It was taken by the Arabs in the 9th century and chosen as a defensive place as we can tell from the fortress and walls. Reconquered in 1235 by Fernando 3rd when the Arab population surrendered to him. It was declared Historical-Artistic Complex on the 15th May 2012. Iznatoraf’s beautiful historical old town made up of narrow and crooked streets tells the story of its Muslim past. The limitless plant pots decorating the facades and medieval arches are one of the main highlights of these special and beautiful town.

Located between the provinces of Jaen and Cordoba, it is formed by the water of the river Yeguas and it belongs to the Confederacion Hidrografica del Guadalquivir. With a surface of 948 hectares and a capacity of 228,7 cubic hectometres, it can be considered as a medium size reservoir. It is well known among recreational fishermen, however it is mainly used for irrigation and provide the nearby towns and villages with water. It was founded in 1989. Its 948 hectares collects the water from the river Yeguas. The river Yeguas, running between Montoro and Marmolejo, and the reservoir split in two the provinces of Cordoba and Jaen. The river Yeguas feeds the Guadalquivir river and runs from Ciudad Real till Jaen’s province, where it marks the borders of Cordoba. It also acts as a border between Sierra de Andujar Natural Park and Sierra de Cardena and Montoro Yeguas Reservoir belongs to Confederacion Hidrografica del Guadalquivir. It is a reservoir of a medium size and it is mainly used for the production of electricity and irrigation. It is also well known for fishing. It holds fishes such as the black bass, the carp and the boga.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: This spectacular castle crowning the beautiful town of Segura de la Sierra can be seen from miles away. It is said that it dates back from some centuries ago from the times of wars between Romans and Carthaginians. Its origin is Muslim, the first records are found in the year 781 the year that Abderraman I took the town from Abul-Asuar. The area of Segura would be under muslim control till the year 1241, when Fernando III’s troops reconquered it for the Christians and giving the castle to the Order of Santiago. Later on Segura de la Sierra was named Headquarters of Encomienda de Castilla, it had a main role in history at the time. This impressive muslim origin fortress is located on the top of the hill where Segura de la Sierra town stands. After the Christians conquered it for good in the year 1241, Fernando III gave it the Order the Santiago, which made big changes in the structure. In 1244 it was chosen for the Headquarters of Encomienda Mayor de Castilla, and later on the place of residence for Gran Maestre de la Orden de Santiago. The castle is open to the public and it looks great after being through two different restoration works - the first one in the 60s and later on at the end of the 20th century and start of the 21st. In this first approach to the castle we will be focusing in the inside and the landscapes that such a privilege location has to offer.

articles.c: Nature, Sierra de Andujar Natural Park
articles.x: There are several paths running through Sierra de Andujar Natural Park, allowing us to enjoy on of the best Mediterranean forests in the whole country. This mountain range is well known for having the biggest amount of the endangered Iberian lynx. It also offers spectacular walks through grasslands, paths, such as the Jabali-Encinarejo’s, of small/medium difficulty but with an enormous landscape and natural value. There is a short but spectacular path from the Jabali’s recreational area, running into one of the best preserved Mediterranean woods in the whole country. From the starting point we could see a granite sculpture of a wild board, granite is very common in the area and we will find it later on in the shape of ‘bolos‘ (‘pins’) Along the 3 kilometres of the path we will cross a beautiful oaks grassland, we will walk next to a stream feeding the Jandula and we will see Encinarejo’s reservoir; one of the oldest reservoirs in the Guadalquivir’s basin. It was created during the second Republic for hydroelectric production. We will end up this family friendly tour, in another recreational area, this time, Encinarejo’s.

Jaen’s province was one of the Republican bastions till the end of the civil war, that explains the amount of air-raid shelters scattered all over it. Some of them, such us this one in Arjonilla, has been refurbished and opened to the public for us to have a close look to the horror of war. In times of war, Arjonila’s authorities used the bell in the Encarnacion’s church’s bell tower, to warn people about a possible danger. The main entrance of the gallery we are visiting today, 170 meters long in a zigzag shape, was located right next to this church. This shelter was founded and restored in 1998. It was built next to the Encarnacion’s Chuch – thinking that the national troops wouldn’t bomb anything close to a church (they were wrong). Today 170 meters of this zigzag gallery built 3 meters deep in the ground can be visited. In the corridors we find entrances to other side galleries – today blocked – that were directly connected to many of the close by houses. During the route we would observe some of the graffiti in the walls, made by the people who excavated the shelter using picks and shovels. Arjonilla was on the republican side during the civil war. It suffered up to 5 raids, so they had to remove Encarnation Church’s top of the bell tower, so that it couldn’t use to point at it from the air.

Sierra Magina Natural Park holds the highest peaks in the province. Miramundos (meaning ‘look at the world)’ shelter is 2077 meters high, and it offers spectacular views of Jaen’s province and beyond; allowing us to see Sierra Nevada, Sierra de Baza or Sierras de Tejada, Almijara and Alhama Natural Park. To get up there we will take the path from Canada de las Cruces; and it is a hard route as part of it is shared with the path to Magina’s Peak. After going through a high incline level we will finally arrive to Miramundos; our reward, not just because of the beauty of the path we followed to come here, but also the remarkable sight to our eyes when we get to the shelter, pure luxury to our senses. From here, we could come back using the same path that took us here, or we could carry on following the path till Magina Peak, with 2167 meter high is ceiling of Jaen’s Province. Miramundos’ shelter is located at 2077 meters high and offers spectacular views over Jaen’s province and beyond. From Miramundos we could see Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Park, Sierra de Andujar and other mountain ranges outside Jaen such as, Sierra de Baza, Sierra Nevada or Sierras de Tejeda, Almijara and Alhama’s Natural Park. Part of the path we take to go to Miramundos is shared with the path to go to Magina’s Peak – with 2167 meters high is the ceiling of Jaen’s Province – so this route is not an easy one due to the high incline level. The shelter has been refurbished lately by the Mountain Club ‘Amigos de Miramundos’. Currently it is in good conditions, and it holds an annual visitors book collecting all visitors’ comments.

The Aliseda recreational area is located in an spectacular natural environment. The Rio Campana path starts from here in a short but lovely walk that will allow us to enjoy the leafy wood that grows next to the river. We could also visit the ruins of an old bath place from the beginning of the 20th century, it used the waters of several hot springs in the area; or La Olivilla, an Iberian linx centre. La Aliseda is located next to the mount under the same name, in an area that for centuries as been very well known by its landscapes and medicinal waters. It is the perfect place to enjoy a picnic in an outstanding natural environment, it has tables, bbqs and play zones for the little ones. The Rio Campana path starts right next to it. It is a brief but remarkable round route of less than 1 kilometre long and low difficulty. In our way we will find oak trees, ash trees, alder trees, and a group of huge stone pines. We will enjoy the leafy wood that grows next to the river. Autumn and spring would be the best seasons to do this route, because the river has more water during this time. This walk is also a reference for mushrooms collectors.

The discovery of new findings in the digging works at the Iberian - Roman archeological site of Castulo, is constant on a daily basis. This is done by Forum MMX project -with archeologists and volunteers - whose target is to bring back to the surface the old Roman Forum of the town. During these works in the latest years, there have been several discoveries that have gone viral around the world. One of the most relevant was the Mosaico de los Amores (Loves Mosaic) named as one of the 10 most important discoveries in the year 2012 by the National Geographic Society. In our second visit to Castulo we check the daily works taking place under Forum MMX’s project. This project, which results have already surpassed all the expectations thanks to some volunteering job, is dedicated to bring back to the surface the Roman Forum of the town. The latest years of findings of great value have taken Castulo’s name along the planet. Probably one of the most relevant ones would be Mosaico de los Amores (Loves Mosaic) - it was considered as one the 10 most important discoveries by the National Geographic Society in 2012- and best preserved; it’s 12 meters long and 6 meters wide, and it shows different scenes representing love, death or seasons. The mosaic is opened to visitors now. It is sheltered under a structure shaped like the original building.

Monte de la Sierra park around build-up areas, best known as “Canada de las Hazadillas” is one of the mountain range more visited by the people from Jaen. Within its more than 6600 acres we can enjoy a natural environment equal to other best known natural park in our province. Otinar and its thousand treausures, Quiebrajano’s reservoir, Cruz de la Chimba’s shelter and Madronales High Pass are some of the most relevant sites. In fact, from the last one, we would be able to enjoy the amazing views of Quiebrajano’s Valley. It is a 1086 meters high Mountain Pass within the more than 6600 acres of Monte de la Sierra park around build-up areas. Close to the recreational area of “Canada de las Hazadillas” there is a small path taking us to Los Madronales. From the highest top we would enjoy the wonderful views of Quiebrajano’s Valley. During our walk we will enjoy the beauty of this mountain range located approximately 20 Kilometres away from Jaen, we could even extend our walk to the Cruz de la Chimba’s shelter.

There is a circular path 150 meters away from Pegalajar that runs through the hillsides of Serrezuela de Pegalajar. It is remarkably well preserved and it is full of information panels along the way. We can enjoy lovely views of Sierra Magina or the meadows using the different viewpoints scattered in its 7 kilometres long. Crossing a typically Mediterranean forest we will find ‘chozos’ - typical building used in this area as shelter for farmers and shepherds - or ancient graffiti in the rock among other things. It is on the way from the Siete Pilillas paragliding station - called after a close by fountain under the same name - and it is considered one of the best areas in Andalucia for paragliding. Starting at that station we will follow a perfectly preserved path throughout the hillsides of Serrezuela de Pegalajar. Crossing a typically Mediterranean forest - mainly planted Aleppo pines - we will enjoy lovely views from Sierra Magina meadows and Pegalajar. Some of the surprises that we will find in our way are the ancient graffiti in rock shelters and ‘chozos’, rough stone circular buildings used as shelters by farmers and shepherds. Due to the beauty of this path, we have divided it in two parts. This is the first one.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: The present ruins of Santo Domingo’s Church belongs to the Renaissance temple commissioned by Francisco de Cobos in the 16th century, replacing the previous church in the same site built centuries before right after the Christian Reconquest of La Iruela. Located inside the castle walls and next to the theatre, which was built emulating the classic Greek theatres, the ruins remind us of the unfinished church of Santa Maria de Cazorla. The group made by the castle, the church and the theatre, is framed by a remarkable natural environment and it is a compulsory visit for those travelling through Sierras de Cazorla, Segura and Las Villas Natural Park. It was originally built after the Christian Reconquest of La Iruela, and in the 16th century, the old Santo Domingo’s Church was replaced by a new one in Renaissance style. Francisco de Cobos was commissioned for this new building, in which disciples from the great Andres de Vandelvira worked. Its complex location - due to a very steep conditions of the terrain and the fact that it is holding ancient structures - was elegantly solved by building a temple with a similar floor plan to the nearby Church of Santa Maria de Cazorla. It was set on fire and looted in June 1810 by French troops while fleeing, leaving the church in ruins. It has been used as a cemetery till 1954. A theatre has been recently built next to it, emulating classical Greek style. Numerous cultural events takes place here in this beautiful location.

San Ildefonso’s crypt occupies practically the same extension as the church itself, from the entrance till the altar. The entrance is in Vicente Montuno, however they are not open to the public at the moment. The Catacombs, holding the remains of martyrs, saints and wealthy people at the time, are specially well-known for being the location which the Renaissance artist Andres de Vandelvira chose for his eternal rest. He was buried wearing the tunic of hermano mayor of the Vera Cruz’s brotherhood. Located under the church, San Ildefonso Catacombs occupied the same extension as the church itself from entrance to the altar. Looking like a maze, after the last restoration works the walls are full of closed niches, harbouring the remains of martyrs, saints and the wealthy people of the time. The crypts are specially well-known for being the place where the remains of the great Renaissance artist Andres de Vandelvira rest for eternity. There is a plaque indicating the exact place where Vandelvira remains are, however it is not the original place where he was buried. It was moved at the beginning of the 17th century with the relocation of Virgen de la Capilla’s lady chapel.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Natural entrance to Sierra de Segura, La Puerta de Segura is a compulsory way in order to access a big number of its towns and villages. It welcomes us with a beautiful path near the Guadalimar river and its clear water that divides the town in two. La Puerta is surrounded by a remarkable natural environment. La puerta de Segura is one of the natural access to Sierra de Segura and compulsory place to get to most of its towns, no wonder it is called like that (Segura’s door). The origin of a settlement here goes back to Islamic times, when Bujalamed Castle - today just remains of a tower) was built. There is a lovely path running by the Guadalimar river that splits the town in two. We will walk this path on this document. The path was built in the 90s and it is provided with a ship - shaped bridge that links both sides of the town. It also holds the traditional flea market every Friday.

articles.t: Palacio de los Duques de Medinaceli
articles.x: The actual Palace of the Duke of Medinaceli is made by 2 buildings made in different styles and dates. The Castle of Don Men Rodriguez, known as Pallares Castle, stopped being used for military purposes after the Reconquest, and today it is part of the Duke’s Palace. The integration of this building in the complex provides with a mixture of opposite styles - Renaissance and Medieval - making the whole monument a special flavour. The Palace is being used as Castellar Town Hall since 1998. Today Duke of Medinaceli’s Palace and Pallares Castle form one single monument. Pallares Castle loses its military function when the Christian reconquest finished, and it is being used by the descendants of the Benavides line -the last lords of the area- in order to build a donjon and a parade. During the 18th century it will get to the hands of the Duke of Medinaceli, and it will be named after him. It is remarkable the blend of different styles, mixing the refined and detailed style of the Renaissance style (that can be found in the palace) with the rough and military ones found in the donjon at Pallares Castle. It has been used as a casino and as the Headquarters of the Circulo de Labradores, but today the Palace holds Castellar’s Town Hall, and the donjo holds the Iberian Museum of Castellar.

The Donjon was built in the 14th Century by the Orden of Calatrava as part of De la Villa Castle located at the top of the city of Martos, a spectacular defensive structure together with De la Pena Castle. The Donjon has 3 floors. The entrance is on the middle floor via a stone stairs attached to it. There is an ‘aljibe’ (cistern) in the low ground which was used to collect rain water from the terrace via a conduit system. It was declared Monumento Historico in 1985 and today holds a history of Martos museum. Martos was conquered in 1219 by Fernando III and given to Orden de Calatrava in 1228, after this, it becomes a border city and one of the main defensive places of Granada Kingdom. Its strategic location pushes the reinforcement of the walls and the building of an espectacular defensive structure made up by two castles surrounded by a walls’ system that will enclose the city. La Pena Castle is build on top of La Pena de Martos, overlooking the meadow, while De la Villa Castle is placed at the bottom of it, the highest place in the city. There are still remains today of some of De la Villa Castle’s walls and some of its towers such as The Donjon, Albarrana Tower and Almedina Tower. The Donjon is remarkable, a 3-floors tower of square base originally with an ‘aljibe’  (cistern) collecting rain water using a conduit system. The Donjon, after the restoration, is very well preserved. It is possible to visit it as well as enjoy the views of Martos from the top of it.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: This little but magnificent reservoir is located in Santiago-Pontones, at the heart of Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park. It is fitted in pinewood covered mountains, and the pines reach its shore. Anchuricas offers a lovely path from the source of La Toba and allows us to walk all the way along the reservoir till the dam. It was built in 1957 to provide water to Miller’s power station. This little reservoir collects the water from Segura River at La Toba. The fact that it is fitted in the magnificent pinewood covered mountains, makes it look like more like a natural pond in the rocks rather than an artificial reservoir. Under the water is located the old little village of Las Casicas, from which the old church is the only bit visible today. The changes of light influence the different colours of the water: blue, turquoise and emerald green. It is an incredible show to look at its silhouette from the top of the nearby mountains such as Puntal de la Misa or Umbria de los Aguijones.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: La Iruela’s castle is located on top of a very steep rock, so abrupt that it makes the fortress unassailable, this explain the fact that the walls are thin. It was built in times of Muslim Rule and was conquered by the Christians in the 13th century, making it bigger and being used as Templar’s headquarters. Declared Historical Monument in 1985, it is one of the most spectacular castles in the province of Jaen. La Iruela’s Castle is located on top of a very steep rock, so abrupt that it makes the fortress unassailable. It was built in times of Muslim Rule and was conquered by the Christians in the 13th century, making it bigger and being used as Templar’s headquarters. It is made up by three enclosures at different levels. The donjon is located in the highest part where we can enjoy the views of the amazing landscapes. Declared Historical Monument in 1985, it holds inside its walls Santo Domingo’s Church. The church was built by the Franciscan order de los Cobos after Santo Domingo de Silos, patron Saint of La Iruela.

Otinar has always been a land rich in water and sediments, perfect for agriculture and hunting. Main reason for the first inhabitants to settle here sheltered in the valley. Veleta Hill’s Dolmen is one of the several prehistoric remains in the area - there are 44 documented rock paintings. Located at the entrance of the settlement at Veleta Hill, the Dolmen was both sheltering the deads and protecting the living ones. Located at the entrance of the settlement in Veleta Hill, the Dolmen used to shelter the deads and protect the living ones. Anyone who dared to enter, should do it among the deads. It is made up by 6 rectangular stones of different heights, topped by a single 2,70 meters wide by 1,70 meters long stone. The entrance is oriented to the East. It no longer standing high because the top stone is at floor level. Looted several times, it is known that the one in 1947 was done as per Otinar Baron’s orders. It is also documented the existence of other dolmens in the valley - looted and destroyed around 1965, they were located not far from the Quiebrajano’s River and in the Brincola gully.

Ariza’s Bridge is one of the most important engineering works by the Renaissance master Andres de Vandelvira. It was built between 1550 and 1560, and went under an important refurbishment during 1868 in which the ground was rectified in order to lower the ramp’s inclination and re-building of the starlings (cutwaters). It is under the water of the Giribaile River since 2010, only to be seen on periods of drought, showing its 100 meters long and its 5 round arches (each of them with a different light). Its preservation is in danger at the moment because it was built in sandstone, and there are many groups asking for its immediate relocation. Ariza’s Bridge was built in the 16th century over the Guadalimar River, and it is one of the most important engineering works by the Renaissance’s master Andres de Vandelvira. It was commissioned by Concejo de Ubeda in order to improve communications with Castilla, and sponsored by Diego de los Cobos y Molina, bishop of Jaen.
