The almost 100 meters long bridge is built in sandstone, ‘lomo de asno’ type, because it’s not completely flat, but it is made of two ramps a bit steep. It is made up by 5 round arches with different light, the highest is 17 meters just at the top of the central arch. At the moment, this beautiful piece of Renaissance engineering can be seen only during drought periods. After being covered by the water of the Giribaile swamp in 2010, its preservation is in danger. It needs to be moved urgently and this is one of the main petition by many groups.

Located approximately 3 Kms away from Porcuna, Cerrillo Blanco is one of the most important archeological sites from the Iberian times, not just in Jaen’s province, but also in the whole peninsula. At the archeological site we can visit the necropolis of burials from the 7th century BC - made up by 24 single burials pits and one megalithic burial - which was still in use till the 1st century BC when the Roman burial style was adopted. The other big discovery of the archeological site, the group of Iberian sculptures  made by more than 50 high quality sculptures, can be seen both at the Museo de Porcuna and at the Museo Provincial de Jaen. Located in the city of Iboica —as Porcuna was known in Turdula times— the archeological site Cerrillo Blanco takes the name from the light colour of the ground. The archeological site is made by a necropolis of burials dating from 7th century BC and by one of the biggest and more important Iberian sculpture found in the peninsula. The works started in 1975 and since then more than 50 sculptures have been found —plus 1400 fragments— representing animals, mythological beings, warriors, hunting or fighting scenes, religious rituals, etc. They date back to the 5th century BC and the stone used —white sandstone— was taken from the quarry of Santiago de Calatrava, south from Porcuna. A century after being made the sculptures were destroyed and buried under big stones. Today they can be found at the Museo Provincial de Jaen and Museo de Porcuna.

Sabiote was a walled town with six entrance gates, only three of them are preserved. In 1931 the castle was declared Historical Monument, and in 1982 the wall was declared Historical - Artistical Group. Despite the damage caused by the French troops, the restoration works are giving back little by little the full splendour that once had. Influenced by Renaissance Italian fortresses,it is the oldest example of Renaissance castle fortified with bastions preserved in the whole country. The inside was severely damaged by lootings and bombing by Napoleon’s troops. However, the restoration works that took place provide visitors with a very good idea of the majesty of the most important military construction in the province during the 16th century. Declared Artistic Monument in 1931, in this second issue we will focus on the inside.

articles.c: Monuments, Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Although the history of Puente Genave village is kind of new, there is proof that this area being occupied in ancient times, for instance the Old Bridge, built in the 1st century BC in order to improve the links between Castulo and Cartagena. It still allows the ‘puentenos’ (name for the locals from Puente Genave) to cross the river, linking the two parts of the village. Guadalimar river, feeding the Guadalquivir, divides the village in two parts, making a beautiful landscape blending nature and urban together. River Guadalimar splits the village in two when it gets to Puente Genave, blending water and nature within the urban center. Although the village was founded in 1933, its origins date back to the 1st century BC when the Romans built Puente Genave as part of the logistics which linked Castulo with Cartagena. Built in stone - alternating stone and masonry - it has just one lowered arch which is remarkably well preserved. The Old Bridge is one of the emblems of this beautiful village, which also offers a wonderful stroll along the river bank of one of the biggest sources feeding the Guadalquivir River. New Bridge is right next to it. Dating back to the 19th century, it was built big enough to allow traffic and relief a bit the work of the Old Bridge.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: In the year 1396 Villanueva del Arzobispo splitted from Iznatoraf, becoming a complete independent Villa. La Moraleja - its previous name - held the Virgen de la Fuensanta’s Sanctuary, well known at the time as a pilgrimage place. The temple, built on site of a previous castle of which two towers remains, has been managed by different religious orders but the Trinitarians are the current residents. There is a very popular legend about the wife of Iznatoraf’s Arabic king. The Sanctuary is held inside an old medieval fortress from the 13th till 14th centuries, from which two towers are still preserved in the present structure. Placed in ancient border lands -and also political instability- this sancturay is considered one of the oldest in the country, as it was a popular pilgrimage place in 1291. It is made by 3 naves, the central one is the biggest. It was built in Gothic style, although it preserves some Romantic details. Various religious orders occupied the temple throughout history: Carmelites, Basilians and Trinitarians since 1884. It is the worship temple for Virgen de la Fuensanta, patron saint of the Four Villas: Villanueva del Arzobispo, Villacarrillo, Iznatoraf and Sorihuela del Guadalimar. On the 8th September she is taken out in romeria (a pilgrimage festivity).

articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Well known for its magnificent castle, not many knows, that Segura de la Sierra holds one of the few remaining Arabic baths that has been preserved till today. With direct access from the Caballeros Santiaguistas Street, they are made by 3 naves making the cold room, warm room and hot room. Restored in 1971, they date back to the 11th and 12th centuries. Situated in the middle of an urban area in Segura de la Sierra, there are one of the few Arabic baths still preserved in the province. To visit them we will have to go down Calle de la Iglesia, finding the entrance in Calle Caballeros Santiaguistas. They are made by 3 naves linked to the typical muslim baths rooms: the cold room -outside one- the warm room and the hot room -inner one-. After being used as a residence, they were restored in 1971. The origin is probably in the 11th and 12th centuries, a flourishing time in this beautiful place.

We could define the Sun’s Cave as the best viewing platform to discover Otinar’s Valley. Full of rock shelters, Otinar hide treasures that tell us about the first inhabitants in this area. The Sun’s Cave is one of those treasures, a huge rock shelter holding ancient rock paintings dating back to the Copper Age. Several scattered dots, some figures and suns representations in dark red decorates the walls of what could be a sanctuary used by the ancient inhabitants of a settlement in Veleta Hill. Unfortunately the paintings have been looted and damaged and we not enjoy them at their best. Located in one of the multiple and spectacular rock shelters of Otinar Valley, the Suns’ Cave is one of the most beautiful examples of ancient rock painting. A big amount of scattered dots, some figures and dark red suns representations decorate the shelter’s walls, scholars think this could be a sanctuary. This painting dates back to the Copper Age and they are clearly linked to the village that was once placed at Veleta Hill. It is not easy to get to it because of the steep terrain. But from the Sun’s Cave there is a privileged view of the valley. Unfortunately, the paintings - that were remarkably well preserved - have been seriously damaged, preventing us from enjoying them at their best.

It holds a place of huge importance due to its strategic position. Sabiote had always have military fortresses throughout history. A pre-Roman oppidium, a Musulman fortress and a Calatravan castle are the predecessors of the spectacular Renaissance fortress built in the 16th century by Francisco de Cobos, who commissioned Pedro de Vandelvira. Strongly influenced by Renaissance Italian fortresses, he built the oldest example of Renaissance castle fortified with bastions preserved, (in outstanding conditions)in the whole country. The spectacular Sabiote’s Renaissance fortress was built between 1537 and 1549 by Francisco de Cobos, Estate Secretary to Charles I. The actual building used the previous Calatravan castle - built in the 13th century after the conquest of Sabiote by Fernando III - that stood in the place of a Muslim fortress. The fact that Sabiote was already conquered in pre-Romans times - it had an oppidum- shows the strategical importance of this area in order to control paths and ways. It’s located at the shore of Guadalimar’s Valley, a priviledged location to watch the mountains of Sierra Magina and Sierra Morena. In this first approach we will look to the external views.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Hernan Perea’s Fields - also known as Hernan Pelea- is one the most singular place at the Natural Park of Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas. More than 12300 acres located at aprox 1700 meters high, shape one of the biggest high plateaus in our country. Its weather conditions - with extremely long winters - makes it ideal for a specific adapted vegetation without trees, increasing the wideness and isolation feeling. Traditionally linked to pasturing, the Seguran sheep is mainly located in these lands. Located around 1700 meters high, with more than 12300 acres wide, Hernan Perea’s Fields are one the biggest high plateaus in Spain. The hard weather conditions - long winters with frequent snowfalls - explains the absence of trees, increasing the isolated and wideness feeling. Its rich pasturage is kept fresh till mid summer, pasturing of Seguran sheep is mainly based at Hernan Perea’s Fields. Spectacular and hard route it is advised to do it in spring time, avoiding winter and the strong snowfalls that takes place here. Because if its wideness and spectacular landscape we have divided the route in several articles.

Built in 13th century after the city was conquered by the Christians, San Lorenzo was placed in one of the neighbourhoods in the outskirts, next to the city’s south wall. From Medieval origin, it was massively modified during the Renaissance and Baroque, leaving very little from the original church. In 1842 it stops being a parish church, thus starting its fall. During the civil war it was looted and closed down, never opening its doors to worship anymore. It’s been recently refurbished and opened to public by Fundacion Huertas de San Antonio. Today, St Lorenzo’s church is used for a wide range of social and cultural activities. From Medieval origin, it was built in the XIII century after the Christian conquest of Ubeda by Fernando III’s troops. The original church would be massively modified during the Baroque and the Renaissance, specially on the last half of the 16th century, when the side door that can be seen today is carved. In 1740 is added to the parishioners of ‘la collacion de San Juan de los Huertos’. It’s in this time when the main chapel is refurbished and the mudejar roof is replaced by a barrel vault. In the 19th century St Lorenzo’s starts to fall; in 1842 it stops as a parish church but it continues to be used for Sunday mass. During the civil war it is looted, and it is terribly damaged. It was then closed down and never open again for worship. Recently recovered by Fundacion Huertas de San Antonio, San Lorenzo has opened its doors again as a cultural and social centre, with numerous activities.

El Callejon del Gato, la calle del Rostro, la calle Santa Cruz and la plaza de los Huerfanos are some of the most well-known places within the odd web of narrow streets that make the Jewish Quarter in Jaen. To walk them means to get close to the legacy of 12 centuries of Hebrew presence in the city, with universal figures such as Hasday ibn Shaprut, adviser to the Cordoba’s Caliphs, one of the first Spanish-Hebrew poets and pioneer of the so called “Golden Age of the Spanish Jews” . Declared of Cultural Interest, belongs to Red de Juderias de Espana “Caminos del Sefarad” since 2005. The Jewish Quarter in Jaen is made of a maze of narrow and steep streets - located between the old neighbourhood of Santa Cruz and San Andres- it became home for more than 300 families. Jewish presence in Jaen dates from 612, however their arrival was probably much earlier. The Jewish Quarter disappeared as such in 1931, turning into a neighbourhood of Jewish converted into Christianism. In 1483 Jaen will be the place of the third Inquisition Court in Spain. The 12 centuries of Jewish and Converted into Christian Jewish presence left an important legacy in the city. The historical relevance of the Jewish Quarter in Jaen is represented in a very special way by Hasday ibn Shaprut, universal figure and pioneer of the so called ‘Golden Age of Spanish Jews’. Part since 2005 of the Red de Juderias de Espana ‘Caminos de Seferad’, the Jewish Quarter in Jaen is one of the most unknown and less valued of our legacy jewels.

Jabalcuz hot spring and gardens, declared of cultural interest in 2009, is located very close to the capital. This hot spring was first mentioned back in 1594; in 1846 it was declared of public utility, been described as sulphate-calcium and hypothermal water, suitable for gynecological and rheumatic problems. Looking at it now it’s difficult to understand how historical important it was in the social life of Jaen, specially during the 19th and 20th centuries. The first mention of Jabalcuz Hot Spring dates back to 1594, by the end of the 17th century there was already a pond to take advantage of this hot spring. The Town Hall built a path from the capital to Jabalcuz at the end of the 18th century, as well as widening the baths and building some houses nearby. In 1846 it was declared of public utility, as it was sulphate-calcium and hypothermal water, suitable for gynecological and rheumatic problems. Together with the gardens it was declared of cultural interest in 2009, looking at it now it is difficult to understand how important it was in the social life in Jaen during the 19th and 20th centuries. After a million broken promises for its refurbishment and recovering, it seems that finally works have been started by Junta de Andalucia.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: El Yelmo is one of the most iconic mount in the whole Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y las Villas Natural Park. It’s 1808 height and its central location in the shire, makes it possible to enjoy the most amazing views in the whole Natural Park. Especially well known by flying sports, it is in June with the International Air Festival when it shines the most. In the edition of 2014 it brought more than 19,000 people. Placed in Segura de la Sierra, El Yelmo is on the most iconic mounts in Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas National Park. Its 1808 height and its central location in the shire makes possible to enjoy the amazing views from the top, reaching landscapes from Albacete, Ciudad real or Granada. It is very steep on the West side, however it’s possible to reach the top by car using the East side, although it is highly recommended- if weather condition and strength allow it- to enjoy one of the wide variety of paths to the top. The top- filled by communication antennae and a shelter- is famous as a flying sport center, whose fans got a compulsory date on ‘El Yelmo’ International Air Festival taking place at the beginning of June.

Very close to Jimena, in the heart of Sierra Magina Natural Park, it is located this peculiar aleppo pinewood declared Natural Monument in 2001 by Junta de Andalucia. Twisted trunks and rounded top are due to the long live trees - some of them between 100 and 300 years old- and ti the natural evolution, without man work. From this privileged location we can enjoy lovely views of Magina. This ancient aleppo pine forest can be found just a couple of kilometres away from Jimena. Its peculiar looks is due to its natural evolution -without man work- and the long lives of its trees, some of them between 100 and 300 years old. Twisted trunks and rounded tops are in high contrast with the typical shapes of young pinewoods. Declared Natural Monument in 2001, from its location we can enjoy lovely views of Sierra Magina Natural Park.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: La Toba is one of the many little villages in Santiago-Pontones, right in the heart of Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas National Park. With less than 40 inhabitants, La Toba offers an unique landscape where water is the main feature. Located next to Anchuricas reservoir, it is specially well known by the source of the river inside La Toba’s cave, where water springs from the mountain all year round. Located in the heart of Sierra de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, La Toba is a small village belonging to Santiago-Pontones. With a population of 40 inhabitants, La Toba gets its name after a stone’s type very common in the area. It is surrounded by water, right next to it, the Segura river pours water into Anchuricas reservoir. The cold, pure and crystal clear water running through the beautiful streets comes from the source of the river inside La Toba’s cave. An unique landscape, the exuberant vegetation. the continuous sound of running water and the range of blues and emerald green of the Anchuricas are waiting for your due visit.

“Los Caracoles” is one of the wide range of amazing places hidden in Sierra Magina. Here we find some little huts built stone by stone by the stonemasons that used to shelter here during the long working seasons in the area. What made these buildings really special, is the fact that they are built without any mortar, using the ‘dry stone’ technique. This kind of architecture is often related to the old Celtic buildings in Asturias and Galicia. Around 3 kms away from Jimena, “Los Caracoles’ is one of the most amazing corners inside Sierra Magina Natural Park. We will find a few little huts made of stone and raised from rubble. The stones are not joined together using any mortar, it’s built using the ancient building tradition of ‘dry stone’. Built with hardly any tool and without transport, these huts were raised stone by stone by stone masons that used to work and spend long seasons under very hard living conditions. This kind of architecture is often related to the old Celtic buildings in Asturias and Galicia.

From almost any place in the city of Jaen you will be able to see the amazing crests of Almodovar Hill. Between La Mella and Jabalcuz, Almodovar Hill is 992 meters high and holds places loved for the people of Jaen. La Plazoleta de las Armas is a little flat surrounded by almond trees, hawthorns and pine trees where several generations of Jaen’s people have grown up in. Located on top of La Glorieta’s neighbourhood, it is worthy a walk to see the wonderful views it has to offer. Located between La Mella and Jabalcuz, Almodovar hill is well known for its crests that can be seen from any place in the city of Jaen. 992 meters high, this hill is not very high, however it holds very special places for the people from Jaen such as Fuente de la Pena o la Plazoleta de las Armas. Main character in this article, Plazoleta de las Armas is a little flat surrounded by almond trees, hawthorns and pine trees which offers beautiful views of the city. Playing ground, walking area and ‘play hooky’ place for several generations, this place -accessible from La Glorieta neighbourhood- is still a very special place worthy a visit.

The huge presence of limestone and karstic effects make our province full of caves and shelters that were once the home for the people living in these lands thousands of years ago, La Granja’s Cave is an example of this. This rock shelter located at the furthest North of the Aznaitin, 750 meters high, holds rock paintings dating back between 2000 and 5000 years BCE. It is needed to ask for a permit at Jimena’s Town Hall to visit the cave. The Graja’s Cave is located at the furthest to the North of the mountain masiff of Aznaitin, in the park known as ‘la Cimbra’. It is a 6 meters deep and 6 meters wide shelter, which reaches 5 meters in its highest part. On top of its amazing views from its 750 meters high, this shelter holds some rock paintings done between 2000 and 5000 years BCE. Made using pigments taken from blending iron oxide, mud and animal fat; the paintings represents rites and shepherd’s duties. Declared Historical Artistic Monument in 1924, the cave can be visited asking for a permit at Jimena’s Town hall.

From Berber origin, Santisteban del Puerto’s Castle dates from the 9th century. Located on top of a hill at 800 meters high on an amazing 200 meters circular plateau - previous site for Oppidum or Ilurgeia Iberian city- the Berbers raised this castle mentioned in the chronicles of its time as Sant Istiban or Astiban. Located on top of an amazing circular plateau on a hill 800 meters high, Santisteban’s in Castle dates from the 9th century. In this same plateau was located Oppidum - or Iberian city - known as Ilurgeia, conquered by the Romans in 192 AD. From Berber origin, the castle is found as Sant Istiban or Astiban in the chronicles that tells the story of the uprising of the Banu Habil brothers against the emir Abd-el-Rhaman. In 1226 Fernando III conquered Santisteban, putting the casting in Christian hands. During the second half of the 13th century there will be some structural changes in the castle. The North tower and some wall support are the only bits left of this castle, from which location amazing views of Santisteban can be enjoyed.

Torredelcampo’s area holds an important collection of towers or watchtowers scattered around Berrueco’s Castle. During muslim times arabs had watchtowers, such as Olvidada, to watch the path linking Jaen with Arjona. After the Christian conquest of the area by Fernando III the Saint, there is a refurbishment and addition of fortifications, and that was the case of La Muna’s Tower. This article also includes photographs of Aldehuela’s Tower, a site of muslim origins latetly altered by the christians. After Torredelcampo’s conquest by Fernando III the Saint, takes place a castle’s refurbishment and widening in the area -such as the Berrueco- and new watchtowers are built, the Muna’s Tower being one of them. This square based tower is made of two floors covered by pointed vaults. It is very well preserved, it is still possible to see some of the remains of the wall around it. In this article there are also images of the Olvidada Tower and Aldehuela Tower, both of them located a few miles away from Torredelcampo. In the highest part of a 476 meters high hill, Olvidad Tower emerges, a circular based watchtower of Arabic origins used to watch the path linking the city of Jaen with Arjona. A bit farther from Berrueco’s Castle, is located Aldehuela’s Tower, a fortification with forms and shapes similar to those of Muna’s Tower, but no so well preserved.

6 Kilometres away from Rus, it is found one of the most unknown treasures in the province of Jaen. This shrine of visigothic origins - unique in the south of Spain- dates from the 6th and 7th centuries. The site is made of a main cave and two other ones next to it, all of them carved directly on the rock.The main cave - which preserves the beautiful facade directly carved on the terrain slope- was used as a chapel, while the other two were used for baptism and monk’s residence. Situated 6 kilometres away from Rus, the Visigoth rock oratory in Valdecanales was built between 6th and 7th centuries. Made of three artificial caves carved in the rock, the beauty of its facade, directly carved on the terrain slope, is still perceived today. The main cave - where worship took place- it is in the central part. Two arches divide the interior into a three naves’ church. According to the research, the cave on the left hand side was used for baptisms, while the one on the right was probably used as a monk’s residence. This shrine- unique in the south of Spain- was discovered by Rafael Vano in 1968, and it was declared Historic- artistic Monument on 21st March 1970.

Less than a kilometre away from Santisteban del Puerto it is located this special archeological site declared Natural Monument by the Junta de Andalucia in November 2001. It is made by 24 footprints - or ‘icnitas’- belonging to the Archosaurs group, bipedal animals which movements could be similar to those of the kangaroo. The footprints are over 230 million years old and it is one of the few archeological sites of this kind in our country. You can find this Natural Monument less than a kilometre away from Santisteban del Puerto. This 230 million years old 24 footprints,  belong to the group of the archosaurs, bipedal dinosaurs which movements could be quite similar to those of a kangaroo. Archeological sites like this one are very difficult to find, because the material where this animal stepped in- possibly sediments from a river or pond- was afterwards covered by other materials allowing its preservation. However the place is in pretty poor conditions and  with this documentary today we want to show this. We want to raise our voice to claim the actual worth of this place. It is one of the few sites of this kind preserved and after been declared Natural Monument by the Junta de Andalucia 23rd November 2001, it has been forgotten and abandoned completely.

One kilometre from Castellar, on a rocky ledge, stands this spectacular Iberian sanctuary dating from the 4th century BC. The site, known as Altos del Sotillo, has three natural caves that housed the sanctuary. The largest is the Caverna del Ídolo, 32 square metres, next to which lay a man-made esplanade where the faithful worshipped the Iberian deities. Barely a kilometre from Castellar, on a rocky ledge in an area known as the Altos del Sotillo, stands this Iberian sanctuary dating from the 4th century BC. Three natural caves make up the sanctuary, the largest being the Caverna del Ídolo, with an area of 32 square metres. Its core is the Cueva de la Lobera, which had up to five adjoining caves that may have been used as dwellings. In front of the Caverna del Ídolo lay a man-made esplanade of about 170 square metres where the faithful worshipped Iberian deities such as the moon or the goddess of fertility. The sanctuary was laid out on several terraces linked by ramps and monumental stairways. Many bronze votive offerings have been found, human figures and domestic animals between 2 and 14 centimetres tall, which the faithful laid before the gods.

Declared a Historic Monument, Berrueco Castle lies a few kilometres from Torredelcampo, in whose municipality it stands. Built by the Muslims in the 12th century on a singular rocky spur, it played a leading role in the border struggles between Christians and Muslims. After the Christian conquest it was altered, taking on its present structure. In the municipality of Torredelcampo, this castle of Muslim origin was built on a singular rocky spur in the 12th century. In a strategic position, controlling the roads between Jaén, Martos and Arjona, El Berrueco played a leading role in the border conflicts between Christians and Muslims. After the Christian conquest of the area it was altered, taking on the structure that has come down to us. Later, during the civil wars between Henry IV and the rebel nobility, the Castilian chronicles link Berrueco Castle with the mysterious death of Pedro Girón. Iberian, Roman and Visigothic remains have been found, showing that the site was occupied earlier.

On the outskirts of Torredelcampo, it stands out for combining nature and history. Here we find traces of the first settlements in the area and can visit the remains of the Cyclopean wall of the Iberian oppidum, dating from the 6th century BC. The south-west of the hill holds a Visigothic necropolis in which up to 20 graves of different sizes can be made out. To round off the visit, we can enjoy a picnic at the picnic tables, in a lovely natural setting. Next to the town of Torredelcampo, it commands the whole of the surrounding countryside. Cerro Miguelico holds important historical traces of the first settlements in the area. Part of the Cyclopean wall of the Iberian oppidum, founded in the 6th century BC, still survives. From the Visigothic period, around the 6th and 7th centuries, there is a necropolis with about 20 rock-cut graves of different sizes. There are also several graves from the Islamic period, from the 8th to the 9th century, which can be told apart by their orientation. The hill is now laid out as a leisure area, with picnic tables and a wonderful natural setting that make it an ideal place for a day in the country.

This mining village in the municipality of Baños de la Encina lived its heyday in the second half of the 20th century. The boom in mining in the area brought it to 2,700 inhabitants and every kind of service. El Centenillo had a school, a hospital, pharmacies, churches (Catholic and Protestant), a market, a cinema, a casino and also one of the first football pitches in our country; many people say it was the very first. Having visited its mines, in this third instalment we take a walk around the village. Having covered several of its mine shafts in earlier articles, this time we focus on the village. Laid out like the mining villages of the English countryside, it was clearly organised by rank: there were areas of housing for single men, for married workers and for foremen, while the most luxurious areas were kept for the engineers and managers. It grew to more than 2,700 inhabitants, with every kind of service: schools, a library, a cinema, a hospital, a pharmacy, a market hall, a casino and more. It has one of the first football pitches in our country (many people say it was the very first) and some of the first tennis courts. Still lived in today, its houses are mainly second homes. Thanks to its location and low light pollution it is an ideal place for stargazing.

Inhabited since 4000 BC, Otíñar brings together an enormous archaeological and historical heritage and a spectacular landscape. After the Christian reconquest there were several attempts to resettle it, which finally led to the founding of the hamlet of Santa Cristina on the old village of Otíñar. This small hamlet came to have 400 inhabitants and a rather peculiar social structure, since the “owners” held a position of social dominance typical of medieval times. It was finally deserted in the 1970s. Inhabited since 4000 BC, Otíñar is a place of incalculable historical and natural value. A strategic point controlling the way to Granada during the Middle Ages. After the Christian reconquest, efforts were made to establish a settlement here. After several failed attempts and centuries of overexploitation of the forests, in 1826 the old village of Otíñar was finally rebuilt after José Cañada Rojo bought its land. In 1831 María Cristina de Borbón was declared patron of the village, which was renamed Santa Cristina. The social structure of the hamlet was that of a true lordship, as many texts and articles of the time show. An example is the article “La Aldea con Amo” (The Hamlet with a Master), published by Luis Bello in the newspaper El Sol on 29 July 1928. The hamlet, which came to have 400 inhabitants, was finally deserted in the 1970s. The end of subsistence farming and pressure from the owners drove its last inhabitants to emigrate.

A mining village in the municipality of Baños de la Encina, El Centenillo grew to more than 2,700 inhabitants at the height of mining in the area. In this second instalment we look at the rest of its mine shafts, mainly Santo Tomás and El Mirador. In this second instalment on El Centenillo we visit the rest of its mine shafts, mainly Santo Tomás and El Mirador. The high output of silver-bearing galena from its mines did not go unnoticed by foreign companies. In 1867 the Sociedad Especial Minera Río Grande was founded, and later the “Centenillo Silver Lead Mines Company Limited” was registered, both of them English. In 1921 the company was renamed “Minas del Centenillo S.A.”, now registered in Spain. The exhaustion of the seams, together with strong foreign competition, brought mining in El Centenillo to a definitive end in 1963.

articles.t: Hermitage of the Virgen del Castillo
articles.x: From a spectacular position, the Hermitage of the Virgen del Castillo looks out over the whole municipality of Vilches. Standing on the parade ground of Vilches Castle, of which hardly anything remains, the hermitage was built in the 18th century on top of the old medieval church of Santiago. Every 14 August Vilches celebrates the feast of its patron saint, who leaves the hermitage and is carried down in procession to the parish church of San Miguel. Built on top of the old medieval church of Santiago, the Hermitage-Sanctuary of the Virgen del Castillo dates from the 18th century. On the very top of the Castle hill, it offers lovely views over the whole town of Vilches. Vilches Castle stood on this hill; very little of it survives today, because the church of Santiago, and later the hermitage, were built on its parade ground. The hermitage houses the image of the patron saint of Vilches, who every 14 August is carried down in procession to the parish church of San Miguel for the festivities named after her.

A mining village in the municipality of Baños de la Encina, El Centenillo grew to more than 2,700 inhabitants at the height of mining in the area. In this first article we follow a path that leads to the Pozo Nuevo, the last shaft opened here. From its buildings we can enjoy incredible views over the Río Grande valley. About 20 km from La Carolina, though in the municipality of Baños de la Encina, lies the mining village of El Centenillo. Its layout is typically English, because its mines were first worked by foreign companies. In this first instalment (we will devote several articles to it) we follow a lovely path to the Pozo Nuevo, the last shaft opened in El Centenillo, where we can enjoy spectacular views of the Río Grande valley. At the start we come across the “bachelors’ quarters”, built to house the unmarried workers. On the way to the Pozo Nuevo we walk along the old railway bed that linked this shaft with the Santo Tomás one.

On the Paseo de la Estación, its main building was put up in 1920 to house the Provincial Museum of Fine Arts, until then in the Palace of the Provincial Council of Jaén. It now has permanent Fine Arts and Archaeology exhibitions, as well as temporary ones. It stands out for having one of the most important collections of Iberian art in all of Spain. The Provincial Museum began as the old Museum of Painting, founded in 1846, which later became the Provincial Museum of Fine Arts, based in the Palace of the Provincial Council of Jaén. José del Prado y Palacio, who was mayor of both Jaén and Madrid, promoted in 1920 a new building for the Museum on the Paseo de la Estación, where it still stands. In 1969 the Provincial Museum of Fine Arts merged with the Archaeological Museum to form the Provincial Museum of Jaén. The Museum has a main building in the Regionalist style and two annexes added in 1965. The main building holds the permanent Fine Arts and Archaeology exhibitions, while temporary exhibitions are held in one of the annexes. Its Archaeology section has one of the most important collections of Iberian art in all of Spain.

The village of El Guindo lies 8 kilometres from La Carolina, on the road to the mining village of El Centenillo. Still lived in today, its houses keep their original style despite being restored. The village sits next to the El Guindo and La Manzana shafts, two of the most important mines in the whole area. In the municipality of La Carolina, it lies barely 8 kilometres from the town. This small mining village, which had 800 inhabitants in the 1950s, is laid out along the roads to the El Guindo and La Manzana shafts. Many of its houses keep their original style despite having been restored. After the mines of Linares declined, those of La Carolina became one of the country’s leading producers of lead. El Guindo, also known as Los Guindos, is another witness to how important mining was in the north of the province.

This lovely hermitage, in the town of Baños de la Encina, was built at the end of the 17th century on the site of an old wayside shrine. Its sober exterior contrasts sharply with the Baroque exuberance of its interior. Above all, its camarín stands out, with its lavish decoration of painted plasterwork. The Hermitage of Jesús del Llano, built at the end of the 17th century, has one of the most spectacular Baroque camarines in all of Andalusia. The austerity of its exterior contrasts strikingly with the Baroque exuberance of its interior decoration. The camarín, opening onto the nave through a great arch, houses the image of Jesús del Llano. Its lavish plasterwork, in which some authors have counted more than 3,000 motifs, makes its shape practically disappear. In the early 1960s it was restored, and the residence and school of the Apostolic Sisters of Christ Crucified was built against the church, giving it its present appearance.

Arbuniel is never without the sound of water. In the municipality of Cambil, in the very heart of Sierra Mágina, the source of the Arbuniel river lies right next to the small village. In this lovely spot water flows from many corners and is gathered in a man-made pool, which then channels it through a system of irrigation ditches. On the slopes of the Torre de Gallerín hill, the source of the Arbuniel river lies next to the village. The water from the source is gathered in a man-made pool that stores it and carries it along a system of ditches running through the whole village. Next to the source stands one of the four power stations that used the river’s water to produce electricity. This lovely spot has picnic tables, so visitors can enjoy a picnic in a unique natural setting.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierra Mágina Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: Mata Bejid castle lies 5 kilometres from Cambil, towards Huelma. To get there, take the forest track to the Puerto de la Mata and Torres, on the left of the road from Cambil. In a privileged natural setting, this castle held a strategic position controlling one of the many gateways into the kingdom of Granada. Barely 5 kilometres from Cambil, towards Huelma, is the start of the forest track that leads to Mata Bejid castle. Between the Sierra Mágina and the Sierra del Almadén, it holds a strategic position, controlling the pass between the two ranges, one of the many routes into the kingdom of Granada. Of Christian origin, it was built at the beginning of the 14th century. There was another castle of Muslim origin, a little further south, which was abandoned for a better site. Long and rectangular, it has a tower at each of its short ends. Today the ruins of a farmhouse built against the castle can be seen. The spectacular views and a privileged natural setting, known as El Castellón, make this a place well worth a visit.

articles.t: The Félix R. de la Fuente Route
articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: This beautiful route starts at the Félix Rodríguez de la Fuente viewpoint, at kilometre 62 of the A-319 road. Its almost 20 kilometres take us through thick forests and offer wonderful views from the six viewpoints we come across along the way. The whole path is in perfect condition and has many information panels explaining the wildlife and plants of the area. This route of almost 20 kilometres was laid out and opened in 2001 as a tribute to the naturalist. It starts at the Félix Rodríguez de la Fuente viewpoint, beside the A-319 road, which offers wonderful views of the El Tranco reservoir. The path follows the route Félix and the crew of “El hombre y la Tierra” usually took while filming in the Natural Park. On our way we pass as many as six viewpoints with spectacular panoramas, in almost all of which water takes the leading role.

This small hamlet is one of the best-kept secrets of Sierra Mágina. A beautiful corner near Cambil, practically deserted today though in good condition. It stands out for a lovely spring whose water gushes out strongly, forming a pool that lets it out in steps. The whole area is surrounded by a spectacular grove of trees that follows the water down. A few kilometres from Cambil, on the road towards Huelma, lies this small hamlet. Practically deserted today, like many of the old mountain hamlets, its buildings are still in good condition. It stands out for the beautiful Mata Bejid spring, whose flow never runs dry. Just below where the spring rises, a lovely pool forms, with stepped outlets that carry the water into a thick, majestic grove. Its water supplies the town and a small power station, and is also used for irrigation and livestock.

The castle of Baños de la Encina is one of the most spectacular and best-preserved fortresses in our country. Built on the orders of the caliph al-Hakam II, the exact date of its inauguration is known from a stone bearing it, which dates it to 968. Oval in outline, it has 14 towers, barely projecting from its wall, plus a keep that was built on the fifteenth tower in Christian times. Without doubt, a must-see. The castle of Baños de la Encina, or Burgalimar castle, is one of the most spectacular military fortresses not just in Spain but in all of Europe. It was the caliph al-Hakam II who ordered it built; the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid keeps a stone, or inaugural plaque, from August 968, the date of its inauguration. This oval castle had fifteen towers, one of which was replaced by the present keep in Christian times. After the first Christian conquest, by Alfonso VII in 1147, the castle changed hands between Arabs and Christians many times, remaining in Christian hands for good from 1225. This fortress, the best-preserved fortified complex from the time of the Caliphate of Córdoba, is one of the emblems of this beautiful Jaén town and of the whole province.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: The Cerrada del Utrero is one of the best-known routes in the park, thanks to its well-kept path, its short length and a spectacular landscape. The Guadalquivir squeezes into a narrow gorge, dropping steeply in a short distance while we walk above its waters. On this walk we can also enjoy the spectacular Linarejos waterfall, a fall of more than 60 metres that ends in a lovely pool. The Cerrada del Utrero is one of the shortest routes in the park and yet one of the most beautiful. A clearly marked path leads us to the waters of the Guadalquivir, which flows squeezed into a narrow gorge. After a ten-minute walk we are beside the small Cerrada reservoir. From here the water runs down steep slopes to the El Valle power station. At this point we can see how the narrow gorge has opened up and its walls have grown very tall, forming a spectacular landscape. In view, too, is the famous Linarejos waterfall, a spectacular 60-metre fall that we will cover in another article.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: In the heart of the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, the Tranco reservoir stands out as the largest in the province, holding almost 500 hm³, and one of the oldest. Yet its importance goes beyond its use as a reservoir: it is a resource of enormous ecological and scenic value. It is well worth stopping at the many viewpoints around it to take in the commanding presence of its waters set among the mountains. El Tranco is the largest reservoir in the province of Jaén, and one of the largest in Spain, with a capacity of 498 cubic hectometres and an area of 1,500 hectares. In the centre of the Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, it is fed mainly by the waters of the Guadalquivir. Of fundamental scenic and ecological importance to the Park, El Tranco also offers active tourism in the form of water sports. A small island rises from its waters, known as Bujaraiza island because it holds the remains of the castle of the same name.

In Baños de la Encina, Peñalosa is a site more than 4,000 years old belonging to the El Argar culture. This beautiful settlement, built entirely of slate, lived off the metal resources of the mines of Sierra Morena, rich in copper ore. In Baños de la Encina, on the shore of the Rumblar reservoir, lies this site more than 4,000 years old. Peñalosa is a Bronze Age site whose activity centred mainly on the metalworking of the area’s resources. In the settlement, built of slate, different levels can be made out, linked by narrow streets. On the lowest level, right by the water of the reservoir, the walls that bounded the settlement can be clearly seen. According to several studies, it was abandoned around 1600 BC.

The Casa de las Heras, also known as the Clock House, is a beautiful Modernista building put up in 1906 by the municipal architect Antonio Merlo. Clearly influenced by Catalan Modernisme, it also has Neo-Mudéjar details. Its ground floor was a shop and its upper floor a home. The Casa de las Heras, popularly known as the Clock House, stands at number 1 Calle Maestra, on the corner of Plaza Santa María. A singular Modernista building put up in 1906, its ground floor was a shop and its upper floor a home. These days the Clock House is in the news again in Jaén. The neglect it suffers, like most of our heritage, has shown itself in new cracks that make its ruinous state even more evident. From here we join the people of Jaén in demanding that the authorities concerned protect our heritage.

Popularly known as “la mella” (the gap), this natural wall is one of the emblems of the city of Jaén. The notch in the middle of its spectacular rocky crest earns it this affectionate nickname from the people of Jaén. Easy to see from almost anywhere in the city, its “crest” offers wonderful views over the whole of it. Rising to 1,244 metres, the Mella hill is famous for its ridge, or “crest”. This natural wall between the Almodóvar hill and the Morteros hill is one of the emblems of the city of Jaén. It is popularly known as “la mella” for the gap, or notch, in the middle of the ridge. From it we can enjoy splendid views over the whole city and some of the nearby peaks.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: The ruins of Santa María are part of an ambitious project for a great church that was never finished. The work, in a marked Renaissance style, took place during the 16th century and is attributed, though not with complete certainty, to a disciple of the master Andrés de Vandelvira. Among its peculiarities, it is the only church built over a river, the Cerezuelo, which was channelled through a vault running beneath the church and the Plaza de Santa María. In Cazorla, the ruins of Santa María are the legacy of a project for a great church that was never finished. Although the exact date of construction is unknown, everything suggests the work was carried out during the 16th century. In a marked Renaissance style, many of its details recall the great master Andrés de Vandelvira, although it may have been one of his disciples who led this great work. It is the only church in Europe built over a river, the Cerezuelo, whose waters were channelled through a vault. After the devastating effects of a great storm, and even fires started by Napoleon’s troops during the Peninsular War, today only a doorway, the chancel, the outer walls and one of the west towers survive.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: Coto Ríos is a small hamlet of fewer than 400 people in the municipality of Santiago-Pontones. Its spectacular position, right in the centre of the Cazorla, Segura and Las Villas Natural Park, makes it a tourist landmark. With just under 400 inhabitants, Coto Ríos is a hamlet belonging to the municipality of Santiago-Pontones. In the very heart of the Cazorla, Segura and Las Villas Natural Park, it is the park’s tourist hub in summer. The Guadalquivir runs past this small hamlet, which lies on its right bank, leaving spectacular landscapes in its wake. It is an ideal starting point for visiting some of the most beautiful parts of the Park.

The landscape of Linares shows how important mining has been to the city. From the mid-19th century it grew exponentially, its population multiplied and the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Belgium opened consular offices there. Mining ended altogether in 1991; paths such as the one to the Mimbre mine keep alive the memory of an activity that transformed the town. The Mimbre mine path starts at the hermitage of the Virgen de Linarejos and passes the San Luis smelter, the Calvario mine, the Mimbre mine and the San Vicente shaft. One of the mining railways of Linares ran along this path, served by the old Linares–Los Salidos railway. The Mimbre mine is one of the oldest in the area, already producing a great deal in the 17th century. Its impressive chimney, 40 metres high, can still be seen today. The San Vicente shaft, 1,008 metres deep, is the deepest in this district. It is especially remembered for the tragic accident in which 6 miners died during the mine’s last haul. May this article be a tribute to them, and to all the lives cut short by the extreme hardship of mining.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: Cazorla enjoys a spectacular setting, surrounded by great mountains and crowned by the splendid La Yedra Castle. This fortress of Arab origin stands out for its sobriety and excellent state of preservation. Its keep takes the leading role, rising more than 30 metres, with walls 4 metres thick. An essential visit, the castle now houses the Museum of Arts and Customs of the Upper Guadalquivir. More than 800 metres up, crowning the town of Cazorla, stands La Yedra Castle. It dates from the 11th century, when the Muslims built the fortress on the remains of Roman fortifications. After the Christian conquest in 1232, the castle was altered and enlarged many times. Above it all stands the keep, whose square plan has also earned it the name of the “Castle of the Four Corners”. It is now in perfect condition and houses the Museum of Arts and Customs of the Upper Guadalquivir.

The Ibero-Roman city of Cástulo is one of the most important archaeological sites in all of Spain. The settlement goes back to the Neolithic, although the city’s heyday came in Iberian and Roman times. The best-preserved remains belong to the latter, such as the baths of the Villa del Olivar or the famous Mosaic of the Loves, which make this a must-see. Five kilometres from Linares, the first settlement of the Ibero-Roman city of Cástulo dates from 3000 BC. Under the Iberians, Cástulo was of great importance, considered the capital of Oretania and one of the largest oppida in Spain. From the 3rd century BC the city passed into Roman hands, and the best-preserved remains date from that time, such as the baths of the Villa del Olivar or the famous Mosaic of the Loves. The city began to decline in Islamic times, until it was completely abandoned in the 14th century. In 2014 the number of visits to the site doubled and important finds were made, such as the figure of a lion that turned up in the excavations of the north wall.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: The last stretch of the Borosa route holds an unrivalled collection of breathtaking landscapes. We will see falls 170 metres high, waterfalls that form beautiful pools whose depth is hard to guess, and the impressive, emblematic Salto de los Órganos. To end the walk we can relax while taking in the dark tones of the Aguas Negras reservoir, in contrast with the turquoise of the water in the Valdeazores lagoon. A tremendous spectacle for the senses. This last stretch, which starts at the power station, is probably the most spectacular and also the hardest. After a few steep climbs, on the left, a fall of more than 170 metres drops from the Picón del Haza. We recommend visiting in spring or during the thaw to enjoy it. Climbing on, through constant zigzags, the Borosa runs over countless waterfalls. One of them, not visible from the path, forms a beautiful pool more than 15 metres deep. The greatest wonder of the route awaits at the Salto de los Órganos: a beautiful waterfall of more than 60 metres that will leave an unforgettable picture in our memory. Finally, after crossing the Picón del Haza through tunnels dug into the rock, we reach the Aguas Negras reservoir and the Valdeazores lagoon.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: One of the main tributaries of the Guadalquivir within the Natural Park, the Borosa river runs through rugged landscapes that form beautiful waterfalls and spectacular cascades. Along the way we pass through areas of lush vegetation: holm oaks, strawberry trees, box, barberry, ivy, brambles and mastic trees line the river. Just before reaching the hydroelectric plant we can enjoy Huelga Nidillo, a spectacular plain that was farmed many years ago. After focusing on the Cerrada del Utrero in the previous instalment, in this one we cover the way to the hydroelectric plant. A tributary of the Guadalquivir, the Borosa is spectacular all along the way, with one fall and waterfall after another. The walk is especially beautiful in spring, when the thaw swells the river considerably and the roar of the water is with us all the time. Just before reaching the hydroelectric plant, a spectacular plain known as Huelga Nidillo awaits, from which we can look up at the southern part of the Banderillas range.

articles.c: Nature, Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas Natural Park
articles.x: For its singular scenic beauty, the Borosa river route is one of the best known in the Cazorla, Segura and Las Villas Natural Park. The spectacular walk through the Cerrada de Elías, an impressive U-shaped canyon the Borosa river has bored into the rock over time, leaves pictures etched for ever in the memory of its visitors. The many pools the river forms along the way make it an ideal place to visit in summer and enjoy the cool waters of the Borosa. The route along the Borosa river up to the Valdeazores lagoon is probably one of the most spectacular in the whole Cazorla, Segura and Las Villas Natural Park. On our way we pass through an impressive canyon, narrow and sheer-sided, known as the Cerrada de Elías. A wooden walkway lets us walk above the river and enjoy this incomparable spot. The karst process acting on the limestone makes rainwater filter down from the heights and seep out through countless cracks in the walls. Because it is so spectacular, we will divide this route into several articles.

This beautiful spot, where water keeps us company, lies next to the village of Albanchez de Mágina. The source of the Hútar stream has for many years been a leisure area that, in good weather, fills with people looking for a break from the summer heat. This wonderful natural setting has picnic areas, barbecue spots, a restaurant and a swimming pool. Its water is used to irrigate the nearby vegetable gardens and olive groves. A few kilometres from the village of Albanchez de Mágina, this beautiful spot holds the source of the Hútar stream. Water is the undisputed star, running over gentle falls and forming small springs that shelter thick vegetation. An ideal leisure area for a summer’s day in the shade. It has barbecues, picnic areas, a kiosk and a swimming pool. Its water has traditionally been used to irrigate vegetable gardens and olive groves, and to drive the flour mills.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierra Mágina Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: Albanchez de Mágina is a small village at the foot of the Aznaitín peak, in the very heart of Sierra Mágina. The castle, which presides over the village from above, is one of its emblems thanks to its spectacular position. Of Christian origin, it was built at the beginning of the 14th century. Declared a Site of Cultural Interest, it can be visited, and it is worth stopping to take in the wonderful views it offers. Together with Bedmar’s, this castle was linked to the Order of Santiago. On the first crag of the Sierra de los Castillejos, the castle rules over the village of Albanchez de Mágina from above. Though small, this castle impresses visitors with its spectacular position. Of Christian origin, it was built at the beginning of the 14th century, replacing a Muslim castle of which hardly anything remains. From the top of the castle we can see the contrast between the mountainous terrain and the hills dressed in olive groves. In the distance we can make out Úbeda, Baeza and Bedmar. It was declared a Site of Cultural Interest in 1985.

Pegalajar sits in an incomparable natural setting, in the heart of the Sierra Mágina Natural Park. In La Serrezuela, a 1,000-metre peak next to the village, lies one of its emblems: its caves. Dug into the rock, they stay at a pleasant temperature all year round thanks to the impermeable ground. Recently restored, the caves have been turned into rural holiday lets. They lie in La Serrezuela, a peak of more than 1,000 metres next to the village of Pegalajar. They are one of the emblems of this Sierra Mágina village and a clear example of rural, natural architecture. The impermeable ground keeps the temperature inside pleasant all year round. The caves, once lived in, have been restored and are available as rural holiday lets.

Built in 1965 on the Old Alcázar of Santa Catalina Castle, the Jaén parador is one of the most highly rated in all of Spain. Its look takes visitors back to times past, of castles and battles. A meal in its spectacular main hall is a treat for all the senses. From it we can take in unrivalled views of the whole city of Jaén. The parador was built in 1965 on the old Alcázar Viejo of Santa Catalina Castle. The main hall, with its crossed arches more than 20 metres up, takes visitors back to times past. The look of the building and the decoration of the rooms were designed in keeping with their surroundings. The legend of a ghost in room number 22 is well known.

Made up of three clearly distinct levels, the castle covers a total of 3,000 square metres. The present parador was built on top of the old castle, or Old Alcázar. The New Alcázar is the best-preserved part of the castle and can be visited since it reopened. The enclosure has six towers, above all the impressive keep, with three floors and almost 40 metres in height. The latest works turned the keep into a museum, where we can enjoy an audiovisual show on the history of Jaén and of Santa Catalina Castle. Santa Catalina Castle is made up of three castles or alcázars: the new castle, the old castle and the castle of Abrehuy. The parador was built on the old castle, or Old Alcázar. The upper level is the new castle, the part that can be visited and the best preserved. It has six towers: the Vela tower, the tower of the embrasures, the Ladies’ tower, the albarrana tower of the Chapel of Santa Catalina, the albarrana tower and the keep. The last stands out, almost 40 metres high and with three floors. The albarrana tower of the Chapel of Santa Catalina houses, as its name says, a small chapel with the image of Saint Catherine of Alexandria, patron saint of Jaén. The parade ground, reached through a gate with a pointed arch, is the part that has been altered most. Since the castle reopened it can be visited, giving access to the dungeons beneath it.

On the Santa Catalina hill, the Castle dominates the city from more than 800 metres up. A symbol of identity for everyone in Jaén, this fortification, whose present form dates from Christian times, has its origins in Iberian fortifications that stood on the hill. With the keep recently restored, the Castle has reopened, letting us enjoy a lovely guided tour through all its centuries of history. Santa Catalina Castle rises on the hill of the same name, about 820 metres up, dominating the whole city. The first defences on the Santa Catalina hill date from Iberian times. From the 8th century on, the Muslims rebuilt the fortification and enlarged it several times. Remains of the Arab wall that ringed the city still survive. Many gates now gone are documented, such as the Puerta de Martos, the Puerta del Sol and the Puerta de Granada, among others. The Castle as we see it today is Christian. After Ferdinand III conquered the city in 1246, several alterations gave rise to the New Alcázar and the keep. The Castle is one of the emblems of Jaén, and this is the first of the three articles Lugares Míticos de Jaén devotes to it.

La Charca is the emblem of Pegalajar, a beautiful village in the Sierra Mágina district. This pond has been essential to the development and economy of the village, watering the olive groves and vegetable gardens through a system of irrigation ditches. With origins in the Middle Ages, La Charca began as a simple reservoir and has become the centre of life and leisure for the people of Pegalajar. After overcoming drought caused by the overexploitation of the aquifers, it is once again looking splendid. The emblem of Pegalajar, in Sierra Mágina, La Charca shows how much water has meant to the development of the village. Since medieval times it has gathered the water from the source of the Fuente de la Reja. That water was used to irrigate the olive groves and vegetable gardens of Pegalajar, which it reached through an extensive system of ditches. The mills, mentioned as early as 1465, were also driven by water from La Charca. The aquifer dried up in 1988 because of overexploitation, leaving La Charca without water. A plan to recover it began in 2007, and today it looks splendid again, with this inscription on one of its walls: “I who gave life demand in justice that you do not let me die”.

articles.c: Monuments, Sierra Sur, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: Jaén is a land of castles and battles: its strategic position between the old kingdoms of Granada and Castile led to the building of many fortifications. Among them stands out the Castle or Fortress of La Mota, in Alcalá la Real. On a hill more than 1,000 metres high, it is one of the largest walled enclosures in all of Andalusia. It was declared a national monument in 1913. It stands on the hill that gives it its name, 1,033 metres up, in the municipality of Alcalá la Real. The complex follows the classic model of the Muslim city, with separate enclosures for defensive, residential and religious purposes. The watchtower-castle, built in the 11th century, marked the border between the kingdoms of Granada and Castile for many years. In 1341 it passed for good into Christian hands, and until the fall of the kingdom of Granada it received large endowments from Castile; afterwards it was abandoned. It was occupied by French troops in the 19th century, who did serious damage as they fled at the end of the Peninsular War. It was damaged again in the Spanish Civil War.

Las Chorreras is one of the best-known spots in Valdepeñas and in the whole Sierra Sur. This short path, which runs alongside the Vadillo river from its source, keeps a spectacular landscape for its visitors. Water, the undisputed star of the walk, rushes down, rests in small pools and falls over beautiful waterfalls. The path, which weaves in and out of the water, is covered in thick vegetation that adds to its beauty. A walk to enjoy, barely 1 kilometre long, right next to the town of Valdepeñas. This lovely spot lies on the edge of the town of Valdepeñas de Jaén. The Vadillo river shapes this small ravine, barely a kilometre long. The path runs alongside the head of the river, letting us admire the pools and waterfalls carved by the crystal-clear water. Thick vegetation that turns the path green and the soothing sound of water keep us company on this short but charming walk.

This spectacular spot lies in the municipality of Puente del Obispo, barely 15 km from Baeza. The lagoon, man-made, was used to store water for irrigating the immense olive groves. Today it is an area of great ecological value, home to a wide variety of birds sheltered by the riverside vegetation around the water. Visitors have hides from which to watch the birds, such as gadwall, common pochard, purple swamphen, teal and little grebe, among others. A few kilometres from Puente del Obispo, this Natural Site covers 206 hectares. Although man-made and tied to the farming of the area, the lagoon has become an ecosystem home to a rich variety of wildlife and plants. Fed by the Torres river, the water covers more than 25 hectares, making it the largest freshwater lagoon in the province. Around it grows the characteristic riverside vegetation that shelters a rich birdlife, including ducks, common pochard and purple swamphen, among many others.

El Piélago is a beautiful natural spot in Vilches, and one of the 28 Natural Monuments in all of Andalusia. A spectacular landscape of great granite boulders over which the waters of the Guarrizas river tumble, forming two large waterfalls. Besides its natural value, with an important flora and birdlife, El Piélago has great historical value. The Via Augusta, which linked Rome with Cádiz, ran through it. The Vadollano bridge, built in the 3rd century BC, bears witness to it, and its remains can still be visited. In Vilches, El Piélago is a spectacular spot that the Junta de Andalucía declared a Natural Monument in 2003. The landscape is made up of great granite boulders over which the waters of the Guarrizas river leap, forming two lovely waterfalls. The Via Augusta ran through it, linking the capital of the Roman Empire with Gades, today’s Cádiz. The Vadollano bridge, built in the 3rd century BC, was part of that road. It was built to cross the drops of El Piélago, making it easier to carry the metal from the mines of Sierra Morena.

articles.c: Nature, Sierra de Andujar Natural Park
articles.x: The Sierra de Andújar Natural Park lies in the north-west of the province of Jaén, in the very heart of Sierra Morena. The Jándula river and its two reservoirs make up one of the most spectacular landscapes in the park. On the way to the Jándula reservoir we come across the remains of the buildings of La Lancha, the village that housed the men and women who built the dam. An area of immense ecological and scenic value, the Sierra de Andújar Natural Park stands out for its wildlife, whose undisputed star is the Iberian lynx. The Sierra de Andújar Natural Park lies in the very heart of Sierra Morena. The Jándula river, a tributary of the Guadalquivir, runs through the park and flows into the reservoir that bears its name. The dam was completed in 1931. More than 1,000 workers took part in building it, living in the village of La Lancha. In the article we can see the ruins of some of the houses of the village, now abandoned. An area of immense ecological value that alternates riverside ecosystems with dehesa pastureland, it is especially famous as one of the last refuges of one of the most beautiful and most endangered animals, the Iberian lynx.

This two-stone flour mill started working in 1540 and for many years was the only working mill in Valdepeñas de Jaén. It has been restored by the “Molino Alto de Santa Ana” association and is in perfect condition. Visitors can see it at work and also enjoy the ethnological museum housed in the mill itself. The so-called Molino Alto de Santa Ana was the first mill in Valdepeñas de Jaén. After the conquest of Granada, the Sierra Sur of Jaén began to be settled, making use of the land where the Arabs had left systems of channels and irrigation ditches. This two-stone flour mill began grinding on 15 August 1540, driven by the waters of the Vadillo river. Restored and kept by the “Molino Alto de Santa Ana” Cultural Association, the mill can be visited and has a lovely ethnographic museum.

Known as “El Neveral”, the Santa Catalina peri-urban park is a green lung of almost 200 hectares next to Jaén. A usual place for hiking, climbing, walking or simply relaxing in its recreation areas, it hides spectacular corners and offers lovely views of the city. Along the paths that cross the park we can walk at the foot of the walls that once ringed the city, discover its many natural springs and let ourselves be carried away by the beauty of the trails through its dense pine woods. Next to the city of Jaén, the Santa Catalina peri-urban park is made up of the hills of “Santa Catalina, El Neveral, La Imora and El Almendral”. Covering almost 200 hectares, the park is a true green lung for Jaén. It has picnic areas, a play area for the youngest and several paths that run its whole length. Walking through the park we can stroll at the foot of the walls that ringed the city, look up and enjoy the castle, or take in wonderful views of the city.

This beautiful spot lies barely 10 kilometres from Jaén, next to Puente de la Sierra. The canyons are the work of the Eliche river, which over thousands of years has bored a beautiful, narrow gorge. A traditional leisure area for the people of the capital, they are ideal for a cool dip in the hot Jaén summer, and also for canyoning or hiking. A few kilometres from Jaén, next to Puente de la Sierra, Los Cañones is a beautiful canyon bored by the Eliche river over time. The spot is ideal for canyoning, hiking or simply a dip in fresh water in one of its pools. It has been one of the favourite leisure areas of the people of Jaén, although today it is so neglected that walking through it is dangerous. At the start of the canyons is the old fish farm, now abandoned, where trout used to be bred.

It stands in the very centre of Jaén, the area the noble and powerful families of the time chose to live in, close to the Cathedral and to other civic institutions. The palace was the residence of Constable Miguel Lucas de Iranzo, after whom it is named. Although it was heavily remodelled in the 19th century after the Casino Primitivo bought it, it still keeps original features, above all its wonderful Mudéjar hall and a lovely courtyard with two arcaded galleries. Constable Don Miguel Lucas de Iranzo made this palace his residence in 1462. Of the original palace only a few rooms, a courtyard and the famous Mudéjar hall survive. The palace covered a large area: several chronicles place it between Plaza de la Audiencia, Calle Maestra, Calle Colón and Calle Cerón. It was heavily remodelled after the Casino Primitivo bought it in the 19th century. In fact, the façade we see today dates from 1920. It now houses the Municipal Culture Board of Jaén City Council.

On Plaza de la Merced, in the very heart of the old town, the Palace of Captain Quesada Ulloa follows the model of the 16th-century noble town house. It is set around a main courtyard, and its tower, with a pair of brick twin windows, stands out. Along the façade we can see remains of ornamentation, with emblematic details and coats of arms of the time. Recently restored, it now houses the Urban Planning Department of Jaén City Council. The Palace of Captain Quesada Ulloa stands next to the church of La Merced, in the very heart of the old town. It was built in the mid-16th century as the home of Captain Fernando de Quesada Ulloa, alderman of the City and corregidor of Cádiz, Jerez de la Frontera and Gibraltar. It follows the model of the 16th-century noble town house, set around a central courtyard. The tower at one end of the building stands out. It housed schools and other public offices, which left it badly deteriorated. Since its restoration it has housed the Urban Planning Department of Jaén City Council.

Concordia Park stands next to Plaza de las Batallas, in the very centre of Jaén. Luis Berges planned it in the 1927 Expansion Plan, which radically changed the face of the city. Covering almost two hectares, the park is made up of four rectangular walks and a central one, closed in a semicircle by a drive beside the gardens. Well known for its duck pond and its old bicycle track, the former La Victoria park changed its name in 2009 under the Historical Memory Law. Next to Plaza de las Batallas, the former La Victoria park took its current name in 2009 under the Historical Memory Law. The park was conceived in 1927 as part of the city expansion plan drawn up by Luis Berges, although work only began after the Civil War. The park covers 16,489 m² and has four rectangular walks and a central one, closed in a semicircle by a drive beside the gardens. The bicycle track and the duck pond have marked the childhood of many generations of people from Jaén.

Almost at the edge of our province lies the Despeñaperros Natural Park, one of the smallest in Andalusia by area but of enormous scenic, natural and historical value. The Cimbarra waterfall is proof of it. This lovely fall of more than 20 metres is formed by a fault running across the Guarrizas river. A wonderful setting for a pleasant walk in the countryside while taking in a unique landscape. Two kilometres from Aldeaquemada, it is one of the best-known spots in the Despeñaperros Natural Park. La Cimbarra is a waterfall more than 20 metres high, caused by a fault running across the bed of the Guarrizas river. On the way to the waterfall we walk through a dense riverside forest rich in alders and ash trees up to 25 metres tall. Beyond its natural and scenic value, near La Cimbarra we can also visit many rock art sites.

Picnic areas, natural springs, barbecue spots, benches and above all a wonderful natural setting have made the Cañada de las Hazadillas one of the leisure areas the people of Jaén visit most. It lies barely 20 km from the capital, inside the Monte de la Sierra peri-urban park, which covers more than 2,700 hectares. Several generations of Jaén children have grown up playing in the old wooden forts of “la Cañada”, enjoying nature at its purest. The “Cañada de las Hazadillas” is one of the most popular leisure areas for the people of Jaén. It lies in the Monte de la Sierra peri-urban park, barely 20 kilometres from Jaén. It is common to see people from Jaén filling bottles at its natural springs. Its picnic areas, benches and barbecue spots make it an ideal place to spend the day. It also has a nature classroom for 60 people. Many people from Jaén will have enjoyed the old wooden forts as children.

The Chimba mountain shelter, well known to Jaén’s hikers, lies very close to the Cañada de las Hazadillas. From there we can set off along the way, enjoying a wonderful setting full of rockrose, rosemary, terebinth and pine. In less than an hour we will reach the Chimba shelter, 1,154 metres up, with spectacular views over the Quiebrajano valley. This small shelter stands 1,154 metres up, near the famous Cañada de las Hazadillas. Easy to reach and in a setting of singular beauty, it has become one of the most walked routes in the Sierra Sur. From the shelter we can enjoy wonderful views of the Quiebrajano valley, Otíñar and, in the distance, Jabalcuz and Jaén. Facing us, majestic, stands La Pandera, 1,872 metres high. We can lengthen the walk by way of the Matamulos hill, which gives wonderful panoramas of the Quiebrajano reservoir, Ventisqueros and Las Coberteras.

On Calle Almendros Aguilar, in the heart of the old town of Jaén, the San Lorenzo Arch is one of the jewels of the city’s heritage. It was part of the ancient church of San Lorenzo, built between the 13th and 14th centuries and demolished in 1825. Inside there is a chapel with a brick vault whose walls are covered with a beautiful Mudéjar tiled dado and plasterwork. Upstairs there is a large hall with a pointed brick dome, where we can also see a plasterwork arch and several noble coats of arms. Tradition has it that the body of King Ferdinand IV, who died in Jaén on 7 September 1312, lay in state here. One of the jewels of the city’s heritage and, paradoxically, very little known. It is the only trace left of the old Church of San Lorenzo, built between the 13th and 14th centuries and demolished in 1825. It was declared a “National Monument” by Royal Order in October 1877, after coming close to being demolished altogether. Its restoration began in 1969 under the Jaén architect Luis Berges. Since 1982 the association “Amigos de San Antón” has looked after the monument. Inside there is a chapel with a brick vault whose walls are covered with a beautiful Mudéjar tiled dado and plasterwork. Upstairs there is a large hall with a pointed brick dome, where we can also see a plasterwork arch and several noble coats of arms.

The washhouses of La Fuente de la Peña are an emblematic place in Jaén, being among the few that survive, and water still springs there. At the start of the road to Jabalcuz, they take us back in time to see what life was like at the beginning of the last century: stones worn by washing on them all year round, with water that comes straight out of the mountain, very cold. La Fuente de la Peña also watered the many vegetable gardens in the area, and it was a usual meeting place for the people of Jaén in the last century, not least because it was on the way to the Jabalcuz spa. There is also a legend linked to the spring: “The ghost of La Fuente de la Peña”. Built in 1906, the washhouse of La Fuente de la Peña stands on the edge of the Glorieta district, on the way to Jabalcuz. Recently rebuilt, it tells of life at the beginning of the 20th century, when there were no machines and women came in the mornings to wash the clothes. La Fuente de la Peña is a natural spring that supplied the washhouse and also provided water for the market gardeners of the area to irrigate. In very rainy years we can also see water springing from the so-called “Ojo del Buey”, about 300 metres from the washhouse towards Jabalcuz.

At Puente Tablas, a few kilometres from Jaén, lies the only Iberian city settled in the Guadalquivir valley. The Oppidum was built during the 7th century BC. We now know it was an aristocratic city of Iberian princes, where the princes’ clients also lived. The whole site is surrounded by a wall and has a single entrance, known as the Puerta del Sol. At this gate, which had two towers on each side, a stele of a female deity, possibly devoted to fertility, has been found. The Oppidum, or Iberian City of Puente Tablas, was built in the mid-7th century BC. The city is ringed by a thick wall, easy to make out from a distance. Research has shown that it was an aristocratic city of Iberian princes. Recent excavations uncovered a palace of about 400 square metres, the only one known in all of Andalusia. The only known entrance to the Oppidum, called the Puerta del Sol, has a stele of a female deity, possibly devoted to fertility.

Because of where it lay, Jaén was constantly overflown by the Nationalist air force, most of which was based in the south of the peninsula.
