After the tragic bombing of the city by the German Condor Legion in 1937, which killed 159 people, a plan was drawn up to provide shelters for the population. The air-raid shelter under Plaza de Santiago was one of them. With room for more than 1,000 people, it was restored in 2011 and is in perfect condition. Work on the air-raid shelter under Plaza de Santiago began after the bombing of 1 April 1937, which killed 159 civilians. With room for more than 1,000 people, the shelter was built under the square, making use of the crypts of the Church of Santiago. Jaén had more than 30 shelters, some of which survive, such as the one at the San Juan de Dios Hospital or the one in this article. When this article was made there was an art exhibition by the Ákaro collective, whose works can be seen in some of the photographs.

articles.c: Nature, Monuments, Sierra Mágina Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: The new castle of Bedmar stands on the Peña Marta, in the upper part of the village. Bedmar lay on the border between Christian and Muslim territory, so it changed hands between Arabs and Christians many times. For that reason, in 1411 the Order of Santiago built the new castle, since the old one could not be defended properly against the constant Muslim attacks. Today Bedmar Castle, declared a Site of Cultural Interest by the Junta de Andalucía in 1985, is in ruins for lack of upkeep. The new castle of Bedmar was built in 1411 by the Order of Santiago. Bedmar held a strategically important position, on the border between Christian territory and the Kingdom of Granada. That led to the building of the new castle, using the latest advances of the time in fortification: zigzag walls, a double enclosure, side entrances and so on. Now in private hands (and up for sale), the castle is in a sorry state of repair.

articles.c: Nature, Monuments, Sierra Mágina Natural Park, Castles and Fortresses
articles.x: From its privileged position, Cuadros Tower gives visitors a wonderful view over the south of Bedmar. Next to the Cuadros sanctuary, this cylindrical tower, 12 metres high, has recently been restored and can now be visited. Inside it was divided into three rooms, the first of them a small store. As a curiosity, it was built with stone from two different quarries, which gives it a striking two-coloured look. Twelve metres high and 6.37 metres across, the tower or watchtower of Cuadros probably dates from the early 14th century. On the north-east of the Carluco hill, the people stationed here kept watch over the southern flank of Bedmar. Recently restored, it can be visited, and you can climb to its terrace to take in some spectacular views. Near the tower there was a rural castle, of which nothing remains, although it is mentioned in medieval texts.

Four kilometres from Bedmar, in the Sierra Mágina Natural Park, lies Cuadros. Known for having the largest oleander forest in the whole peninsula and one of the largest in Europe, Cuadros is a place where the beauty of nature overwhelms the visitor. Following the path that starts at the recreation area, we can visit the source of the Cuadros river, the oleander grove and the Cueva del Agua, enjoying a unique natural setting along the way. Four kilometres from Bedmar, Cuadros is one of the best-known spots in Sierra Mágina. Beside the source of the river we can enjoy one of the largest oleander groves in all of Europe. This oleander forest follows the river, letting hardly any light through and forming natural “tunnels”. Carrying on along the path that starts at the recreation area, beside the oleanders, we can also visit the Cueva del Agua.

La Fuenmayor is a recreation area next to the village of Torres, in the heart of Sierra Mágina. It is an ideal place for a walk in nature and for some peace and quiet, with a picnic beside the pond fed by one of the many natural springs of Mágina. On our visit to La Fuenmayor we will enjoy the soothing sound of water and the shade of great poplars, holm oaks and walnut trees, among others. If you visit in spring, when the cherry trees are in blossom, you will see a beautiful picture of the valley dressed in white. A few kilometres from the Jaén village of Torres, in the very heart of Sierra Mágina, lies La Fuenmayor. Great poplars, holm oaks, walnut trees and hawthorns line a lovely pond fed by one of the many springs to be found in Mágina. La Fuenmayor is an ideal recreation area for enjoying nature, and the starting point of several routes through beautiful landscapes. The picnic tables and stools, made from old millstones, invite us to have a picnic and relax in this wonderful setting.

El Bodegón is one of the most emblematic places in Jaén, a peculiar spot that is both a wine bar and a grocer’s and still keeps the essence of the traditional. In the very centre of Jaén, in an early 20th-century building, El Bodegón awaits at any time of day: for breakfast, for a glass of wine at midday or to enjoy a night out in Jaén. The oldest customers say that there was once a goldfinch called “the innkeeper” that fluttered around inside, ate the crumbs of the tapas and drank from the glasses of wine. In a building put up at the beginning of the 20th century, “El Bodegón” is one of the oldest and most peculiar establishments in Jaén. The premises first held the building’s wine cellars, then became a vegetable store, until it opened as a bodegón during the Second Republic. Today this century-old business is still a grocer’s and a wine bar, where customers of every age come together. The building it occupies has been listed by the Junta de Andalucía as part of the ethnological heritage of Jaén.

The market hall, also known as the “San Francisco Market”, is one of the few traditional markets still trading. Opened in 1870 by Francisco Guerrero, then mayor of Jaén, it replaced the old stalls on Plaza de San Francisco. The original building was rectangular, with the stalls set around a large open-air courtyard and a fountain in the middle. After almost a century and a half, the market still keeps Jaén families company day to day and fills their larders. Opened on 8 June 1870, the market was rectangular, with the stalls set around a large open-air courtyard. It was built on what had been the orchard of the convent of San Francisco, which is why it is also known as the “San Francisco Market”. Of the original building only the Santa Ana gate survives, which leads into the market from Calle de los Álamos and has recently been restored. The market hall breathes the essence of traditional markets, of lifelong shopkeepers, of local produce and, in short, of the history of Jaén.

The San Eufrasio cemetery, known to the people of Jaén as “the old cemetery”, holds 200 years of our city’s history. Many of our neighbours have relatives buried there, and it also holds a mass grave of people shot under the Franco regime. In recent years it has been neglected by one city council after another, and it is now in such a sorry state that in December 2012 it had to be closed because of the danger it posed to visitors. We have recently learnt that the current Jaén city government intends to privatise its management. From Lugares Míticos de Jaén, in our modest work of making our heritage known and calling for its protection, we demand the restoration of a place that is part of our people’s history and we flatly reject its privatisation. This time, Lugares Míticos de Jaén publishes an article with a single photograph. We meant to photograph the San Eufrasio Cemetery, known to the people of Jaén as “the old cemetery”, but we were not allowed to. Jaén City Council forbids taking pictures inside the cemetery. We assume the ban is due to the sorry state of neglect the place is in, which many national media have reported. A place that holds almost 200 years of our city’s history, where many of our neighbours have relatives buried, and which also holds a mass grave of people shot under the Franco regime. This neglect has been going on for many years, and we do not mean to point only at the city’s current government. We point at them and at all who held office before them. We were able to visit the cemetery these days and see for ourselves the deplorable state it is in. Open niches, broken headstones, heaps of rubble piled all over the cemetery, areas fenced off for fear of collapse (some of them propped up with beams)… In short, a grotesque sight for anyone who visits, and even more so for those whose relatives rest there. The cemetery, closed since last December, has been opened for All Saints’ Day, and that is how we were able to visit it. We have now learnt that the City Council intends to privatise the management of the site, which is listed as a Site of Cultural Interest (BIC) and where illustrious figures of our city such as Almendros Aguilar, Ruiz Córdoba, Fermín Palma, José María Tamayo and Bernardo López are buried. From Lugares Míticos de Jaén, in our modest work of making our heritage known and calling for its protection, we demand the restoration of a place that is part of our people’s history and we flatly reject its privatisation.

In the old town, the Arab Baths are one of the emblematic monuments of Jaén. Built by the Muslims during their rule of the city, they date from the year 1002. After the Christian conquest they stayed in use until the 15th century, when they seem to have become a tannery. At the end of the 16th century the Count of Villadompardo built his palace on top of them, and they lay buried until 1913, when they were discovered while the Monumental Catalogue of Jaén was being compiled. Their restoration began in 1936, was interrupted by the outbreak of the war and was not resumed until 1970. It was completed in 1984 and earned the medal of honour of the Europa Nostra association. They were built at the beginning of the 11th century and had four rooms: a vestibule, a cold room, a warm room and a hot room. In the basement of the Villadompardo Palace, they cover 450 square metres, which makes them among the largest in Spain. Despite the Christian conquest of the city in 1246, they stayed in use until the 15th century. At the end of the 16th century the Villadompardo palace was built on top of them, and they were buried. Restoration work began in 1936 but was interrupted by the Civil War. It resumed in 1970 and the restoration was fully completed in 1984.

Where the Susana river meets the Corteses stream stands the old power station of Valdepeñas. The setting has a beauty that is hard to match: falling water in one waterfall after another and lush vegetation make a wonderful sight. Today only the ruins of the station and of the houses its workers lived in remain. Near Chircales, in the upper Valdearazo valley, lie the ruins of the old power station. The water fell downhill from two intakes: the one at the Castellón dam and the one at the dam on the Corteses stream. Harnessing the force of the water, which drove the turbines, was the key to producing electricity. The station was run by the Málaga company “Hidroeléctrica del Chorro”, whose name can still be seen on the back wall.

In the old town of Jaén, the San Juan de Dios Hospital is today the seat of the Instituto de Estudios Giennenses and a usual venue for lectures. Its origins go back to the 15th century, although it was from 1619, when the Order of San Juan de Dios took it over, that it came to be known by its current name. It was the leading hospital in the province and one of the longest-running in Spain, staying open until 1973, the year Jaén’s new hospital complex was inaugurated. Today only the chapel and the original hospital building survive intact, and both have been restored. The youth hostel right next to it was built on one of the buildings of the old hospital, keeping its architecturally valuable façade. It began as the union of the old hospitals of the Holy Mercy and of San Lázaro, which were handed over to the Order of San Juan de Dios in 1619. The complex was made up of two courtyards, a church and the hospital itself, which was enlarged many times. With the last alterations, completed in 1957, it came to cover 12,000 square metres. It remained in use until October 1973, when it handed over its services to the newly opened Princesa Sofía Hospital. In the years that followed the building fell into a sorry state of neglect, until in 1992 it was restored as the seat of the Instituto de Estudios Giennenses.

Seminary Park is one of the two largest parks in Jaén, with more than 3 hectares of green space. Laid out on a slope, the park is made up of several terraces linked by paths. It offers some of the best views of Jaén, with the Cathedral and the Castle in the leading roles. A place to enjoy on daytime walks as well as in the calm of the night, when the park shows another side under the lights of the Cathedral, the Castle and the nearby villages. It is named after the city’s Diocesan Seminary, which stands beside it. It opened in August 1998 and has more than three hectares of green space. From Seminary Park we can enjoy a beautiful panorama of Jaén, made up of the Cathedral, Santa Catalina Castle and the mountains around the capital. The views are as good by day as by night, when the sun sets and gives way to the lights of the main monuments and the mountain villages.

The José Nogué School of Art stands in the heart of the old town of Jaén, on Calle Martínez Molina. The site it occupies once housed the Convent of the Noble Ladies of Our Lady of the Angels, which later became a casino, a barracks and finally a School of Arts. With more than a century of history, the school took the name of José Nogué, who was director of the School and of the Provincial Museum of Fine Arts of Jaén. It was founded in 1887 as the “School of Arts and Crafts” under the Royal Economic Society of Friends of the Country. In 1910 it was officially recognised and renamed the Higher School of Industrial Arts. Later, in 1924, it broke away from the Industrial School and became the School of Arts and Crafts. The School, whose building was rebuilt in the mid-20th century, stands on Calle Martínez Molina, on the grounds of a former convent. More recently it was renamed School of Art, in reference to the painter José Nogué, who was a teacher there and its director.

Río Frío is one of the many springs in the Sierra Sur of Jaén that gather the water filtered through the mountains after the winter snows. It has a picnic area that offers cool air and quiet on summer nights, as well as water much prized by the people of Jaén. This wonderful spot is about 7 km from Los Villares, on the way to Valdepeñas de Jaén. Río Frío is a spring that gathers the pure, crystal-clear water drained by the Sierra de la Pandera. As well as supplying water to Los Villares and Jaén, it has picnic tables and shade under thick vegetation. A perfect place to rest and relax to the murmur of the water, whose melody keeps us company throughout the visit. For its beauty and uniqueness, it is listed as a site of ethnological interest in the information system of the Andalusian Historical Heritage.

Famous for its signature Rossini and for dishes such as “Migas con Avíos”, La Barra is one of the most emblematic bars in Jaén. Its spectacular decor, crowded with old objects, gives the place a special charm. Above all, La Barra is somewhere to taste fully home-made cooking with dishes of its own. In short, one of those corners where all the senses get an outing. Run by its current owners since 1959, although there has been a tavern on the premises since the early 20th century. For its peculiar decor and its home-made cooking, La Barra is one of the most emblematic bars in Jaén. Its shelves, crammed with bottles and old objects, make a small museum of traditional crafts and customs. The people of Jaén know its “Migas con Avíos” and its signature black pudding tapa only too well. On top of all that, La Barra is the only place in the world where you can drink a Rossini.

Charcoal burning was a common activity in the mountains of Jaén. The wood of holm and gall oaks was the raw material the mountain people used to make charcoal, which made the hard winters more bearable. The Quejigo del Amo, also known as the Quejigo del Carbón, is living proof of that activity. Its scars, and above all the difference in thickness between its branches and its enormous trunk, are clear evidence of the pruning it underwent to produce charcoal. This majestic tree, estimated to be between 500 and 1,000 years old, is one of the largest gall oaks in all of Andalusia. Also known as the Quejigo del Amo, it is more than 500 years old. It stands in the Sierra Sur, at about 1,800 metres above sea level. Its peculiar shape comes from the repeated pruning it underwent to produce charcoal. The marks of charcoal burning show in the difference in thickness between its great trunk and its branches. This majestic tree of singular beauty was declared a Natural Monument in 2001.

The Pitillos canyon, carved by the Valdearazo river over thousands of years, is one of the most beautiful routes to enjoy in the Sierra Sur of Jaén. The impressive canyon, rock formations as peculiar as the chess knight or the Piedra del Palo, and dense, varied vegetation make up a spectacular landscape that ends where the Quiebrajano reservoir begins. Because of where they lie, the upper reaches of the Quiebrajano are one of the most beautiful landscapes in the Sierra Sur of Jaén. The Pitillos canyon, bored by the Valdearazo river over the millennia, leads the way to them. Natural sculptures such as the chess knight or the Piedra del Palo make this landscape, if possible, even more spectacular. Following the route marked by the GR-7, the canyon gradually opens up, showing the visitor the first waters of the reservoir.

In the very heart of the Sierra Sur of Jaén, the Quiebrajano reservoir is much more than a reservoir to the people of Jaén. The natural beauty around it has made it a place of leisure for nature lovers, who gather nearby to climb, hike or simply enjoy the landscape. It lies in the very heart of the Sierra Sur of Jaén, in a privileged natural setting. The rugged ground offers beautiful contrasts, with high peaks such as the Grajales massif or La Pandera surrounding the reservoir. It is fed by the Valdearazo river, which takes the name of the reservoir once it has passed through it. The Quiebrajano reservoir covers 125 hectares and supplies water to the capital and to several other towns in Jaén. After the heavy rains of 2013, the reservoir currently stands at 93.75% of its capacity.

La Alameda is the oldest park in Jaén, with more than five centuries of history. Its full name is Alameda de Capuchinos, because the original owners of the land were the Capuchin friars, who kept their orchards and trees here. Its majestic trees and gardens make a magnificent promenade, a usual meeting place for the people of Jaén. The Alameda de Capuchinos dates back to 1577, which makes it the oldest park in the city of Jaén. It originally lay outside the wall that protected the city, and was reached through the Puerta del Ángel. It has been remodelled several times; one of the most significant changes was made by Dean Mazas, who added a carriage drive. Its lovely gardens and leafy trees make a charming promenade, where the shade offers shelter through the summer months. By day it belongs to the elderly and to children. At night, young people and couples make La Alameda their place to go out.

The haberdashery La Verdadera is one of the oldest businesses still trading in Jaén. Opened in 1934 by the grandparents of today’s managers, it keeps the character of a traditional family business. Its care for its customers, its warmth and its professionalism keep La Verdadera the haberdashery of reference for the people of Jaén after almost 80 years. Opened in 1934 by Juan and Emilia, grandparents of the generation that now runs and works in the shop. First set up on Calle Ramón y Cajal, it now stands on Plaza San Francisco, next to the Cathedral. At La Verdadera you will find a very complete range of wool, thread, embroidery, buttons, lace, ribbons and more. Specialists in Holy Week goods, at La Verdadera they work to dress the Nazarenes and the “pasos” of Jaén in their finest.

articles.x: Thirteen kilometres from the city of Jaén, Otíñar offers a spectacular journey through the traces of the history that has shaped Jaén, from prehistory to the present day. Rock art, a Chalcolithic settlement, a necropolis, Roman remains, an Islamic fortress later turned into a Christian castle by Ferdinand III, and a hamlet founded in 1826 that stayed inhabited until 1970: this is the fascinating journey we invite you on. In the Sierra Sur of Jaén, the Otíñar valley holds many examples of rock art. The engravings (petroglyphs) in this article are in the Barranco de La Tinaja and date from the Neolithic. Inhabited since prehistory, Otíñar was a key enclave during the Middle Ages. Otíñar Castle was built in 1246 on top of an Arab fortification, when Ferdinand III conquered Jaén. It watched over the border with Granada, sending smoke signals that could be seen from Torre Bermeja. In 1826 the hamlet of Santa Cristina de Otíñar was founded, and it stayed inhabited until 1970.

El Turronero is another family business with a history: a shop full of every kind of sweet and treat that has delighted the youngest in Jaén for many years. Birthday piñatas, Christmas mantecados and turrón, the little bags of sweets the Three Wise Men order to hand out in homes across Jaén, and those metal toy cranes that have kept several generations company. Having just turned 30, it is a family business now run by the second generation. It started out as a grocery shop. For a long time now, sweets, nuts and treats have filled its shelves with colour. It keeps Jaén supplied at Christmas with its mantecados, turrón and the little bags of sweets for the night of the Three Kings. On Calle Espartería, El Turronero is one of the youngest customers’ favourite shops. Oh! We nearly forgot: here you can still find those legendary metal toy cranes.

Mimo Libros is an old school book shop, it looks more like a library than a simple bookshop. The magic of literature wraps the visitors from the very moment they step in, the paper’s scent, the high shelves full of books and an atmosphere that invites to relax and chill, a place where the clock stops and the rush is scared away. A place where the paper scent wraps the visitor, an oasis where the old traditional book trade is preserved. Founded on the 14th February 1997, it was part of the Books Guild in Granada, currently in the process of be founded again. It is located at the heart of the historical neighbourhoods of the city, at 13th Capitan Oviedo Street, not far from the well-known Los Jardinillos Square. At Mimo you can find antique, second hand and on sale books, plus documents, engravings and original drawings.

When we talk about Jabalcuz, we are mentioning a reference for everybody in Jaen, it’s not only for its impressive presence in the landscape, but also due to its relevance in history. Its hot spring was the origin of the building of a thermal and touristic center together with amazing gardens and a wonderful natural environment, it makes an ideal place for enjoying strolls and spare time. Located 3 Kilometres away from the city and 1614 meters high, it is one of the main features of our landscape and it is in the heart of Jaen’s people. The first documents about its hot springs dates back to 1594, being the thermal bath built at the beginning of the 17th century. Unfortunately abandoned today, the baths were at their best at the end of the 19th century and beginning of the 20th century. The gardens, of a great landscape and botanical value, offers to the visitor a space for relaxing, enhancing the contact with nature. Jabalcuz’s baths and gardens were declared of cultural interest in 2009.

El Posito Stores with almost a century with its doors opened is the oldest business in Jaen city. It is a place where you will be served in the counter in the traditional way and where the traditional atmosphere of neighbours and locals is preserved. El Posito is the larder of Jaen, its scales and shelves are Jaen’ history witnesses. The opening of the Posito Stores dates to 1912 and 1914. Located in the little square under the same name, is one of the oldest shops in the whole province. It is a shop that still preserves the essence of tradition. They call themselves ‘ the larder of Jaen’. A place where our products are in a priviledged place.
